contested.label: stock, returns, firms, abnormal
contested.why: Event studies mostly find ties raise firm value; C00019 is negative only because its event was bad news for Suharto (implying positive value), leaving the Cheney null (C00197) and the Malaysian crisis loss (W3122513589) as genuine but event-specific dissent.

contested.label: vote, party, incumbent, turnout
contested.why: Same relationship, no framing problem: five studies find benefits raise incumbent support, Uganda grants (C01138) and NREGS exposure (C01241) find the reverse, and C00460 finds Progresa's earlier positive result was a data-merge error, contradicting C00226.

contested.label: vote, elections, polling, station
contested.why: Same relationship (roads, electrification, services and incumbent vote), no framing issue: four studies find a reward, C01172 finds better services cut ANC support, and C00663 finds PMGSY roads had no effect, contradicting C00656 on the same programme.

contested.label: growth, capita, outcomes, income
contested.why: Same relationship (democracy and growth) with democracy the cause in every card: within-country transition studies find faster growth while Barro finds a weakly negative effect and Przeworski et al. none, the classic cross-section versus panel split.

contested.label: elections, vote, municipality, national
contested.why: Same relationship (local migrant or refugee presence and far-right vote), same framing of the cause: three studies of large or sudden inflows find gains while C02108 finds a small reception centre cut Front National growth, a genuine conflict that fits contact theory.

contested.label: infant, death, first, child
contested.why: C01199 is signed on school attendance (which rose) although its infant-death estimate is negative like C00336, so on infant mortality the two agree once flipped; the genuine dispute left is C01908, which finds democracy has little or no effect on infant and child mortality.

gapThemes.title: When do voters reward delivery, via which channel, and for how long?
gapThemes.text: It is unknown when and why voters reward governments for visible delivery (cash transfers, roads, schools, services) rather than ignoring or punishing it, whether any reward comes from gratitude, salience, implementation quality or credit claiming, and whether it lasts once programmes become routine. The field has well-identified single-programme estimates, mostly positive (La O 2012, Manacorda et
gapThemes.why: Transfers, roads and services reach voters together with campaigns, brokers and other benefits, so gratitude, salience, credit claiming and quality cannot be separated, and most estimates are aggregate and cover one programme over a few elections.

gapThemes.title: Do information campaigns and media change accountability at scale?
gapThemes.text: It is unknown whether informing voters, through audits, report cards, debates, text messages or media, durably changes votes and politicians' behaviour once it is scaled up and politicians, parties and media respond, and through which channel (better-informed politicians, selection, salience, attention). The field has many short-run field experiments (Ferraz and Finan 2008, Banerjee et al. 2011, B
gapThemes.why: Experiments are short, small and partial-equilibrium by design, the channels (information, salience, selection) are bundled in one treatment, and fine-grained data on media consumption and politicians' responses are missing.

gapThemes.title: Are voters instrumental, or expressive and socially motivated?
gapThemes.text: It is unknown how far voters act instrumentally (voting as if pivotal, abstaining or switching strategically, coordinating on likely winners) rather than expressively or under social pressure, and which competing turnout model best fits behaviour. The field has well-developed pivotal-voter, ethical and expressive models and some laboratory and field support (Coate et al. 2007, Battaglini et al. 20
gapThemes.why: Voting costs, benefits and beliefs about being pivotal are unobservable in field data, and equilibrium multiplicity lets many behaviours fit the theory, so no design cleanly separates instrumental from expressive motives.

gapThemes.title: How do autocrats keep insiders and local agents loyal and productive?
gapThemes.text: It is unknown why some autocracies build durable institutions (ruling parties, legislatures, formal promotion rules) and select competent agents while others rule through purges and personal loyalty, and how much of what local agents deliver under promotion and quota systems is real rather than manipulated. The field has formal models of power-sharing, purges and coalition formation (Svolik 2009,
gapThemes.why: Autocrats' internal bargains are unobserved, official performance data can be gamed, and the evidence comes mostly from a few settings, chiefly China, so comparative tests of the models are missing.

gapThemes.title: What changes inefficient institutions, and why do they outlast elites?
gapThemes.text: It is unknown what moves a society off inefficient institutions: how elite turnover, coalitions of social groups, non-voluntary change forced by excluded groups and reform backlash combine to decide whether elites, institutions or both change, and where institutions come from in the first place. The field has theory in which weak commitment, fear of replacement and failures of the political Coase
gapThemes.why: Institutions are endogenous, the forces the theories turn on (political competition, elites' attitudes, replacement threats, coalition bargaining) are barely measured, and the models are stylised two- or three-group set-ups with no systematic empirical counterpart.

gapThemes.title: What builds state capacity, and what do investments in it return?
gapThemes.text: It is unknown which forces causally build legal and fiscal capacity (ethnic division, instability, conflict, resource rents, coalitions, legitimacy), why capacity-raising reform is not adopted when models say it should be, how societies exit weak-capacity and clientelism traps, and what specific capacity investments return once measured and scaled. Theory on investment in state capacity is rich (B
gapThemes.why: State capacity moves slowly, is endogenous to the conflict, income and institutions it is meant to explain, and is measured mainly at the country level or by retrospective performance, so causal designs and individual-level evidence are rare.

gapThemes.title: Does accountability select better politicians or discipline them?
gapThemes.text: It is unknown whether electoral accountability improves outcomes by selecting better types into office or by disciplining whoever holds it, and what that is worth in welfare terms, since term limits, term length, disclosure and debates move both at once. The field has natural experiments on term limits and tenure (Alt et al. 2011, Dal Bó and Rossi 2008, 2011) and field experiments on audits and re
gapThemes.why: Selection and discipline run through the same elections and the same treatments, separating them needs rare events such as incumbents surprised by a chance to run again, and welfare effects need outcome data that seldom exist.

gapThemes.title: Which accountability reforms last, and which component does the work?
gapThemes.text: It is unknown which component of monitoring, incentive and participation reforms in frontline services does the work (information or participation, pay or daily monitoring, a single audit element), whether effects persist beyond two years once workers adapt or collude, and how to cut absence at scale. Randomised evidence shows community monitoring, attendance incentives and audit reforms improve d
gapThemes.why: Most evaluations follow treated units for two years or less, interventions bundle several components, and adaptation by workers and officials (collusion, changes in who joins) appears only over longer horizons.

gapThemes.title: How durable are the effects of mobilisation and enfranchisement?
gapThemes.text: It is unknown how long the effects of mobilisation, voting-access reforms and enfranchisement last, whether habits and social spillovers build on them, and who gains from them in resources and welfare. The field has many one-election field experiments and a few well-identified enfranchisement studies (Gerber et al. 2003, Cascio and Washington 2013, Naidu 2012, Cantoni and Pons 2019), but the autho
gapThemes.why: Most experiments measure only the next election, enfranchisement shocks are rare and work through slow channels such as the intergenerational transmission of human capital and wealth, and long individual-level voting panels are missing.

gapThemes.title: What makes people run for office, and can reforms widen the pool?
gapThemes.text: It is unknown what drives the decision to run (motives, costs, family and network ties) and whether competition, training or lower entry barriers improve the candidate pool rather than only the electability of those already willing. Citizen-candidate models under plurality and runoff rules (Besley and Coate 1997, Osborne and Slivinski 1996) and first training and primary interventions (Dal Bó et a
gapThemes.why: The pool of would-be candidates, including non-runners and losers, is rarely observed, models stop at plurality and runoff rules with exogenous parties and no campaign information, and credible variation in entry costs is scarce.

gapThemes.title: Does bureaucratic autonomy raise delivery without political will?
gapThemes.text: It is unknown whether insulating bureaucrats and their overseers from politicians raises delivery when political will is weak, why bureaucracies nonetheless rely on costly rules rather than autonomy, and how patronage and multiple principals shape what civil servants, auditors and regulators do. Civil-service reform and rules change performance and politicians' policy choices (Aneja and Xu 2024, U
gapThemes.why: Autonomy, political will and patronage are endogenous to one another and rarely manipulated, so field experiments that randomise autonomy are scarce and political constraints are documented mostly through cases and correlations.

gapThemes.title: Do limits on political money curb influence or just divert it?
gapThemes.text: Unknown is what spending limits, firm-donation bans, Citizens United, disclosure and revolving-door cooling-off periods do to policy, corruption and the use of other channels (lobbying, dark money, charity, shadow lobbying). Discontinuity work now shows effects on elections and donor types, but downstream policy outcomes and substitution are mostly untested.
gapThemes.why: Reform thresholds identify only local effects on elections, and the covert channels that rules may push money into are unrecorded by design.

gapThemes.title: What carries a historical shock to today's income, and does it fade?
gapThemes.text: It is unknown which channel carries a historical shock (the slave trade, the Scramble for Africa, colonial land tenure, the Holocaust, European settlement) into today's income and trust, and whether the legacy is a self-sustaining equilibrium or a slowly decaying shock. The field has established large reduced-form effects for each shock (Nunn 2008, Banerjee and Iyer 2005, Michalopoulos and Papaioa
gapThemes.why: A single shock moves every candidate channel at once and the intermediate outcomes (state capacity, trust, human capital at earlier dates) are rarely observed, so reduced-form designs cannot apportion the effect.

gapThemes.title: What makes elites concede democracy, and why do transitions cluster?
gapThemes.text: It is unknown what makes elites concede the franchise or lose power, how slow-moving forces (income, education, urbanisation, inequality) interact with the triggers (revolutionary threat, elite rivalry, coordination), and why democratic transitions cluster in time and across regions. The field has a strong cross-country income-democracy correlation that is contested once country fixed effects are
gapThemes.why: Transitions are rare, the slow-moving drivers are endogenous and absorbed by country fixed effects, and the best-identified evidence comes from single episodes (such as Britain's 1832 reform) whose external validity is untested.

gapThemes.title: Does democracy improve schooling and service quality, or the reverse?
gapThemes.text: It is unknown whether and how democratic competition improves the quantity and, above all, the quality of schooling, health and other services, through which mechanism (electoral competition, clientelism, information, decentralisation), and how much of the link runs the other way, with education building democracy or autocrats using it to stay in power. The field has associations and some evidence
gapThemes.why: Regime and education are jointly determined by omitted time-varying factors, cross-country data on service inputs and quality are poor, and political decentralisation cannot be separated from democracy when instruments work through a broad cluster of institutions.

gapThemes.title: Do economic losses or cultural grievances drive populist support?
gapThemes.text: It is unknown which economic shocks (trade, austerity, financial crises, labour-market change) and which cultural or status grievances turn into populist and radical-right support, in which direction the causation runs, and who supplies populist politicians once demand exists. The field has established correlations between globalisation, austerity or crisis exposure and populist voting across US a
gapThemes.why: Voters' subjective economic assessments and cultural identity are jointly determined, shocks such as trade, austerity and migration arrive together, and credible variation and data are largely confined to the US and Europe.

gapThemes.title: How do party gatekeepers and primaries decide who reaches the ballot?
gapThemes.text: It is unknown how parties and voters actually screen candidates, and whether gatekeepers keep women, immigrants and able outsiders off the ballot through discrimination, rent protection or lack of contact. Theory covers how incentives shape selection (Besley 2005) and primary and list-position studies are growing (Galasso and Nannicini 2011, Casey et al. 2021, Casas-Arce and Sáiz 2015, Dancygier e
gapThemes.why: Gatekeepers' choices and the pool of aspirants are not observed, and the adoption of primaries and list rules is itself endogenous, so researchers see only the winners of a selection process they cannot observe.

gapThemes.title: Why does corruption persist in some places and how do others exit?
gapThemes.text: It is unknown what makes corruption higher in one place than another (institutions, culture, development, electoral discipline, expected future rents) and how places exit high-corruption equilibria, including why governments tolerate petty bribery and why rich-country health bureaucracies are clean. Cross-country regressions (Treisman 2000, Mauro 1995), models of misgovernance (Banerjee 1997) and
gapThemes.why: Cross-country corruption data are perception-based and endogenous to income and institutions, and settings with exogenous variation in culture or institutions are rare, so reverse causality and multiple equilibria cannot be separated.

gapThemes.title: Why did states form and build capacity so unevenly outside Europe?
gapThemes.text: It is unknown why states failed to emerge or to build capacity across much of the tropics, Africa and the Americas, and whether the war-driven, fiscal-capacity account built on European evidence, including conflict-driven mass schooling, travels beyond Europe, to democracies and to recent periods. The field has a rich body of state-formation theory and European evidence (Dincecco 2015, Paglayan 20
gapThemes.why: Pre-colonial political and fiscal data outside Europe are sparse and possibly selected (for example the Standard Cross-Cultural Sample), which keeps theory far ahead of evidence.

gapThemes.title: How do media control and misinformation shape dissent and support?
gapThemes.text: It is unknown how rulers, parties and media shape citizens' beliefs and what that does to dissent and regime support: how subtle manipulation (fraud, media capture, targeted social control, repression, misinformation) works alongside formal institutions, how far the information environment is itself endogenous to the regime, and why simplistic or identity-driven beliefs take hold. The field has mo
gapThemes.why: Preference falsification and exposure to propaganda are hard to observe, data on individuals' public political expression are scarce, and nothing shifts the information environment independently of the regime that controls it.

gapThemes.title: Does anti-corruption policy work in equilibrium and in the long run?
gapThemes.text: It is unknown whether audits, monitoring, transparency and enforcement reduce corruption net of substitution to other forms, price responses by remaining bribe takers, entry of criminal organisations and general-equilibrium spillovers, and whether effects last once agents learn or norms habituate. Experimental and quasi-experimental evidence exists on audits, monitoring and information (Olken 2007
gapThemes.why: Audit and monitoring experiments run once, in one place and over short horizons, so substitution, rotation and equilibrium responses cannot be observed without repeated or system-wide designs.

gapThemes.title: Do pay, exams and screening select public workers who perform better?
gapThemes.text: It is unknown whether pay, performance pay, exams and dishonesty screens change who selects into public jobs along ability, honesty and prosociality, whether recruits perform better once hired, and how sorting evolves in the long run. Experiments and sorting studies show that wages and career incentives shape applicant pools (Dal Bó et al. 2013, Ashraf et al. 2020) and that dishonest people sort i
gapThemes.why: Long-run sorting cannot be observed in an experimental sample, performance data on those hired are rarely linked to recruitment arms, and corruption-proneness is hard to measure before entry.

gapThemes.title: Which management practices and incentives raise public-sector output?
gapThemes.text: It is unknown which management practices, assignment rules, mission framing and incentive allocations across the layers of a hierarchy raise public-sector output, which of them is the active ingredient, and why managers do not already adopt cheap fixes such as emphasising the mission. Managers matter for productivity (Fenizia 2022), promotion incentives affect worker output (Deserranno et al. 2025
gapThemes.why: Management, mission and hierarchy design are bundled in real organisations, most studies randomise one practice in one agency, and results from researcher-run programmes may not survive delegation to line managers.

gapThemes.title: Which reformable institutions drive growth, separate from geography?
gapThemes.text: It is unknown which specific institutions (executive constraints, term limits, contracting versus property-rights rules, ethnic or local governance) drive growth, as opposed to institutional quality treated as one bundle, and how their effect can be separated from geography, climate, culture and prior development. The field has established a robust link between institutional quality and income and
gapThemes.why: Institutions come as bundles and are measured by their outcomes rather than by the rules a policy maker could change (Glaeser et al. 2004), and no credible source of exogenous variation moves one rule at a time.

gapThemes.title: How do rural elites turn land and labour control into lasting power?
gapThemes.text: It is unknown through which levers (vote control, employment rents, labour coercion, chiefs' discretion, rent seeking) landed and local elites turn control of land and labour into persistent inequality and underdevelopment, and how much long-run damage runs through that political channel. The field has formal models and historical legacy estimates (Engerman and Sokoloff 2002, Dell 2010, Baland and
gapThemes.why: Elite control works through informal levers that are rarely observed, so researchers can only test implications of specific mechanisms rather than measure vote control, rent seeking or accountability directly.

gapThemes.title: What links public support for democracy to its survival or erosion?
gapThemes.text: It is unknown how popular support for democracy translates into its survival or erosion: what citizens actually mean by democracy, why they tolerate norm-violating incumbents, whether supportive citizens act to defend institutions, how elected populists dismantle competitive elections and media freedom, and how extremist vote shares turn into breakdown. The field has models of voter responses to n
gapThemes.why: Breakdowns are rare, citizens mean different things by democracy so 'support' is hard to compare, and the microdata on who benefits from democratic institutions that would identify the mechanisms do not exist.

gapThemes.title: How can corruption be measured objectively and comparably?
gapThemes.text: It is unknown how to measure corruption objectively and comparably (payment processes, price effects on users, hypothetical tax yield, hidden cheating, political connectedness) when perceptions and victim surveys are systematically biased. Micro studies observe corrupt payments or their direct consequences in one sector or country at a time (Olken and Barron 2009, Bertrand et al. 2007) and cross-c
gapThemes.why: Corruption is illegal and hidden, perceptions are biased, direct observation exists only for narrow settings, and bribe, demand and firm productivity data are rarely matched.

gapThemes.title: Do lobbyists and donors buy votes, access or information?
gapThemes.text: What is unknown is which channel actually moves policy: transmitting information to legislators, buying access, or buying votes outright. The field has well-developed models of informational lobbying and a few empirical tests, but no setting that separates the channels, and the multi-round, multi-expert and dynamic versions are untouched.
gapThemes.why: The information passed to politicians and their informational needs are unobserved, and informational and electoral effects of contributions are intertwined in the same data.

gapThemes.title: How much policy does lobbying buy, and at what welfare cost?
gapThemes.text: What is unknown is the causal return to lobbying spending and contributions (policy won, firm value) and how far lobbying-shaped equilibrium policies sit from the social optimum. Structural estimates exist for trade protection and energy, but pre-legislative effects, wins that merely preserve the status quo, and other policy domains are unmeasured.
gapThemes.why: No design isolates lobbying's causal effect on outcomes, much of what lobbying wins is an invisible continuation of the status quo, and the no-lobbying counterfactual needed to price distortions is never observed.

gapThemes.title: Which channels carry democracy's effects on growth and redistribution?
gapThemes.text: It is unknown through which channels and which specific features of democracy (competition, franchise, constraints, form of government, sequencing with liberalisation) shape growth, redistribution and the size of government, and whether a credible average effect of democracy can be estimated at all. The field has cross-country estimates of democracy's effects on growth, inequality and reform (Acem
gapThemes.why: Few countries switch regime and overlap between treated and untreated is weak, regime measures are blunt and not reproducible, and the firm- and household-level data needed to trace channels are scarce.

gapThemes.title: Do quota effects persist and hold for other designs and countries?
gapThemes.text: It is unknown whether quota effects persist beyond a few electoral cycles, whether permanent reservation entrenches new monopolies, and which designs (reserved seats, zip lists, rules restricting cross-gender competition) work outside Indian village councils. Randomised and close-election studies, mostly in India, Brazil, Sweden and Spain, give credible estimates (Chattopadhyay and Duflo 2004, Bro
gapThemes.why: Identification relies on a rule that creates as-good-as-random variation, usually in one country with a short panel, so quota type, scale and horizon are confounded with place.

gapThemes.title: How to raise tax compliance where third-party information is missing?
gapThemes.text: It is unknown which levers raise tax compliance where informality and weak capacity leave no third-party information (enforcement, consumer rewards, collector incentives, taxpayer loans, legitimacy), how they interact, and whether effects survive beyond two years or scale without pushing firms into informality. Strong experimental evidence exists for single levers, such as performance pay for tax
gapThemes.why: Each study evaluates one lever in one setting over a short horizon, informality and taxpayers' strategic responses are hard to observe, and credible variation in enforcement capacity is rare.

gapThemes.title: Does decentralising or splitting jurisdictions improve provision?
gapThemes.text: It is unknown whether decentralisation, jurisdiction splitting and smaller polities improve the level and quality of public goods, growth and democracy relative to centralised provision, and what they cost in weaker monitoring, local capture, limits to local taxation and lower politician quality. Theory and surveys cover capture, yardstick competition and the fiscal limits of local government (Bar
gapThemes.why: Decentralisation is adopted for reasons correlated with outcomes, direct centralised counterfactuals are rare, and the costs of splitting (monitoring, corruption, politician quality) lack data.

gapThemes.title: Do survey-measured persuasion effects survive real campaigns?
gapThemes.text: Unknown is whether persuasion and advertising effects estimated in survey experiments and short field tests persist to Election Day and carry over to competitive campaigns, micro-targeted media and non-US party systems. Field experiments find small average effects, but studies differ in design and setting, and survey-based message testing predicts real effects poorly.
gapThemes.why: Strategic opponents, repeated exposure and whole-campaign strategies cannot be randomised, and survey and field estimates have not been matched on the same treatments.

gapThemes.title: Do competent or honest politicians deliver better policy, and how?
gapThemes.text: It is unknown whether politicians' competence, honesty and valence change policy and government quality, through the policies chosen or how they are implemented, and whether selecting for competence costs social representativeness. Leaders matter for some outcomes, mainly monetary policy and growth (Jones and Olken 2005), and democracies and quotas change who is selected (Besley and Reynal-Querol
gapThemes.why: Competence, honesty and education come bundled and are hard to measure, close-election designs cannot isolate one trait without post-treatment bias, and quota instruments exist only in a few places.

gapThemes.title: Do quotas raise targeted groups' welfare, and through which link?
gapThemes.text: It is unknown through which links descriptive representation reaches the welfare of the targeted group (targeted spending, party control over renomination, legislators' voice, household take-up) and whether outcomes beneficiaries value actually improve. Reserved seats can shift spending towards the targeted group (Pande 2003) while reserved-seat politicians may still not redistribute (Jensenius 20
gapThemes.why: Welfare outcomes arrive years after adoption and need linked household-level data, survival and migration confound child-health comparisons, and party constraints on reserved-seat politicians are documented mostly through interviews rather than tested.

gapThemes.title: What does corruption cost beyond theft, and who bears it?
gapThemes.text: It is unknown what corruption and connections cost beyond the resources stolen (distorted allocation of inputs, hiring and credit, forgone quality in public contracts, effects on trade) and who bears the losses across income groups. Firm-level effects (Colonnelli and Prem 2021) and credit misallocation inside an elite network (Haselmann et al. 2018) have been estimated, but the authors say causal
gapThemes.why: The evidence is observational, bribes are rarely matched to demand and firms to productivity, and second-best theory cautions against reading misallocation as a welfare loss.

gapThemes.title: What makes some organised interests win: size, structure or rivals?
gapThemes.text: Which groups actually get their demands met, and why, is unknown: group size and concentration, form of organisation, opposition from rival lobbies, or members' wealth (the merely affluent versus the top 0.1 percent). Classic theory (Olson, Becker, Stigler, Peltzman) and correlational evidence on elites exist, but group power is still treated as a taste parameter.
gapThemes.why: Data linking specific groups' demands to outcomes are scarce (so far mostly case studies), and no design separates group size from organisation and rivalry.

gapThemes.title: How do informal norms, ideas and ideology interact with formal rules?
gapThemes.text: It is unknown how informal norms, conventions and ideology interact with formal laws and institutions, and whether ideas have an autonomous role in social change rather than merely reflecting material interests. The field has documented long-lived cultural traits such as trust and social capital (Nunn and Wantchekon 2011, Guiso et al. 2008) and modelled formal institutions in depth, but political-
gapThemes.why: Norms and worldviews are not recorded in historical or administrative data, and no variation shifts them independently of the formal rules and material interests they travel with.

gapThemes.title: Which land and property-rights reforms raise productivity, and how?
gapThemes.text: It is unknown which land and property-rights changes (tenancy reform, formal land rights, cooperative ownership, communal control) raise productivity and welfare, through what mechanism beyond investment and credit, and whether they beat alternatives such as credit or other asset transfers. The field has evidence from individual reforms (Banerjee et al. 2002, Field 2007, Montero 2021), but the aut
gapThemes.why: Large property-rights changes are rare outside social upheaval and the property-rights structure is itself endogenous, while the long panels and linked micro or administrative data that would reveal mechanisms are missing.

gapThemes.title: How can vote buying be measured credibly beyond case studies?
gapThemes.text: It is unknown how widespread vote buying and clientelist linkages are beyond documented cases, because no valid cross-national measure exists that separates vote buying, turnout buying and double persuasion. The field relies on surveys, list experiments and single-country studies (Vicente 2013, González-Ocantos et al. 2011, Wantchekon 2003, Bobonis et al. 2025), whose authors flag conformity and s
gapThemes.why: Respondents and political actors have reasons to hide the exchange, the boundary between vote buying, turnout buying and persuasion is blurred in practice, and survey answers are biased by conformity and social desirability.

gapThemes.title: How do connections create firm value, and what limits extraction?
gapThemes.text: It is unknown through which channels (procurement, credit, regulation, policy information) political connections raise firm value, what alternative rent-extraction routes open when one closes, and why firms deal with government through personal ties rather than formal mechanisms. Connection premia and credit misallocation have been measured in several countries (Fisman 2001, Khwaja and Mian 2005,
gapThemes.why: Connectedness is hard to define and observe when power is decentralised and ties shift, and channels are bundled together in firm-level outcomes so credit, regulation and procurement effects cannot be separated.

gapThemes.title: Do pay and returns to office select honest types or rent-seekers?
gapThemes.text: It is unknown whether higher pay, non-financial rewards such as prestige or civic duty, and the rents of office draw in honest and competent people or mainly rent-seekers, and whether better selection and better incentives complement each other. The field has salary evidence on legislator performance (Ferraz and Finan 2010), a pay-and-selection model (Besley 2004) and asset-disclosure evidence of
gapThemes.why: Pay is endogenous to the type it attracts, honest types are hard to tell from mimics, and adverse selection and moral hazard generate the same observed premium.

gapThemes.title: How do parties motivate, monitor and choose brokers and targets?
gapThemes.text: It is unknown what motivates political brokers, which monitoring mechanisms besides electoral returns let parties discipline them, how parties choose among brokers (unions, priests, ethnic or traditional leaders) and whom they target, including when rival machines compete. Case-based and experimental evidence covers specific brokers and targeting rules, such as Mexican public-sector unions (Larreg
gapThemes.why: Brokers and their contracts are hidden, parties rarely face comparable rivals or monitoring technologies within one setting, and most evidence comes from a few country cases.

gapThemes.title: What durably weakens clientelism: insurance, cash or information?
gapThemes.text: It is unknown whether insurance, cash transfers, information or hiring reform make citizens abandon clientelist ties altogether, through which channel, and whether effects last once programmes scale, repeat or leave Brazil and Uganda. Experiments show that insurance, anti-corruption information and one-off grants shift political behaviour in the short run (Bobonis et al. 2022, 2025, Blattman et al
gapThemes.why: The treatments are one-off experiments or reforms with non-random timing, so durability, scale effects and the channel (misattribution, group socialisation, financial independence) cannot be separated with the evidence at hand.

gapThemes.title: What is a person's total news diet across platforms and devices?
gapThemes.text: What is unknown is how much news individuals consume in total, from which titles and through which devices, because existing work studies one platform at a time and no public dataset follows the same people across newspapers, television and online. The field has platform-specific effects and shares, but cannot say how large media power is outside the biggest outlets.
gapThemes.why: Consumption surveys do not identify titles, browsing and app data sit with platforms, and stories seen on feeds but not read or remembered go unrecorded.

gapThemes.title: Do media-driven shifts in beliefs and votes last and change policy?
gapThemes.text: What is unknown is whether media-induced changes in beliefs and votes persist beyond a year and show up in what governments do and in welfare, not only in turnout or vote shares. Short-run effects on votes and some on public spending are documented, but only four of fifteen reviewed persuasion studies cover horizons of a year or longer, and policy links are mostly inferred.
gapThemes.why: Outcomes that matter for welfare (policy choices, official performance) are measured coarsely, and long-run follow-up of media exposure is rarely possible.

gapThemes.title: Does competition and entry of rival outlets discipline media bias?
gapThemes.text: What is unknown is whether more rival senders, outlets or narratives reduce distortion: whether an ideologically distinct entrant pulls incumbents toward or away from the centre, whether alternative sources discipline reputation-driven bias, and whether viewers switch away when choice exists. Theory yields competition results that depend on commitment, but empirical tests are scarce.
gapThemes.why: Entry and the availability of alternatives are rarely exogenous, and reputation-driven bias cannot be told apart from consumer, reporter or government tastes for distortion.

gapThemes.title: Why do voters comply with clientelism: reciprocity, fear, monitoring?
gapThemes.text: It is unknown what makes voters honour clientelist exchanges, whether reciprocity, an individual propensity to vote, fear of losing an entitlement, deference to local authorities or the risk of being monitored, and which voters are cheapest to bind. Brokers are known to target reciprocal individuals (Finan and Schechter 2012) and responses to clientelist appeals differ across voters, including by
gapThemes.why: Reciprocity, loss aversion, fear and monitoring produce the same observed compliance in most designs, and good individual-level measures of propensity to vote or psychological traits are missing.

gapThemes.title: Do incumbents mix fraud, violence and vote buying, and does it pay?
gapThemes.text: It is unknown how incumbents jointly choose among vote buying, miscounting and violence, which settings (ethnic allegiances, resources, term limits, moderate insecurity) favour each, and whether leaders who use election violence actually stay in power. Formal models of illicit strategies and of why insecure rulers hold elections exist (Collier and Vicente 2011, 2013, Little 2012), as does cross-na
gapThemes.why: Datasets covering violence, miscounting and vote buying together are lacking, ex post outcomes such as regime duration are confounded when proxies like polls or riots are used, and actors hide the manipulation.

gapThemes.title: Do observers, audits and open data curb political manipulation?
gapThemes.text: It is unknown whether domestic or foreign observers, election-timed audits, image-based tally audits, wider polling-station access and public inspection data deter fraud and the political manipulation of service delivery, and when those in power act on the information. Field experiments on monitoring, audits and inspection data exist (Callen and Long 2015, Brollo et al. 2019, Callen et al. 2023, L
gapThemes.why: Most monitoring evidence comes from single interventions in one setting, politicians object to or ignore the data when it threatens them, and forensic tools for auditing other elections are still being built.

gapThemes.title: Does competition limit corruption risk in discretionary procurement?
gapThemes.text: It is unknown through which mechanisms procurement discretion, bidder competition and audit design drive corruption and waste, including for one-of-a-kind goods that make up much of public purchasing, and whether moving from auctions to direct contracts raises prices. Correlations between discretion, competition and corruption risk (Decarolis et al. 2024), a split of waste into active and passive
gapThemes.why: Comparable price data exist only for standardised goods in a few settings, quality shading and unofficial arrangements are unobserved, and discretion is chosen endogenously by agencies and officials.

gapThemes.title: How is influence organised: lobbying firms, coalitions and networks?
gapThemes.text: What is unknown is how the supply of influence is structured: whether firms lobby alone, in coalitions or through hired firms, how lobbying firms are organised and compete, and how groups spread resources across socially connected legislators and across local and national levels. Lobbying research has mostly modelled and measured how much is spent, not who delivers it.
gapThemes.why: Lobbying-firm, client, coalition and legislator-network data have only recently been assembled, and theory has centred on the amount of lobbying rather than its organisation.

gapThemes.title: How do dynasties persist and what do they cost in governance?
gapThemes.text: It is unknown through which channels (name recognition, contacts, family networks, favoured access to jobs) dynasties and political connections perpetuate themselves, and what they cost in policy-making, service delivery and rents outside the few countries studied. Dynastic self-perpetuation in the US Congress (Dal Bó et al. 2008), relatives' rents in Sweden (Folke et al. 2017) and the electoral w
gapThemes.why: Consequences are hard to separate from the selection of family members into politics, records of relatives' careers and local service delivery are rarely linked, and the settings studied may not carry over to less transparent institutions.

gapThemes.title: What does patronage cost in welfare, and when does it deliver?
gapThemes.text: It is unknown what patronage and vote buying cost in welfare terms (incentive, selection and match effects, an oversized bureaucracy, worse service delivery) and when patronage ties deliver services rather than extract rents, for instance only in low-capacity settings. Some costs of patronage hiring are quantified (Colonnelli et al. 2020, Xu 2018) and the same governance resources are shown to ser
gapThemes.why: Almost every comparison municipality or bureaucracy also has patronage, so counterfactuals are missing, and selection, incentive and match effects are hard to separate in one design.

gapThemes.title: What drives regulators' enforcement choices, and who gets leniency?
gapThemes.text: Unknown is how far regulators and enforcers deviate from the rules in applying them, what drives the deviation (donations, capacity, personal discretion, citizen pressure) and what it costs in outcomes. Evidence from US banking, Indian pollution inspections, Chinese pollution appeals and Colombian deforestation shows enforcement varies, but each study covers one industry or country.
gapThemes.why: Enforcement effort and its outcomes (ambient air, water, forest) are rarely observed directly, so discretion must be inferred from noisy outcomes or one-off experiments.

gapThemes.title: How are bribes and extortion priced, centralised and enforced?
gapThemes.text: It is unknown what lets corrupt officials and gangs coordinate and centralise collection, set prices and sustain complex illegal arrangements, what intermediaries do to price discrimination and access, and how users and demand respond to the price of bribes. Bribe payments on trucking routes (Olken and Barron 2009), agent-mediated licensing (Bertrand et al. 2007) and gang extortion (Brown et al. 2
gapThemes.why: Bribes are paid in secret, so prices, elasticities and the role of intermediaries are rarely observed outside a few hand-collected settings, and the counterfactual for limiting bribe takers is missing.

settled: History shapes present institutions and through them economic performance: legal origin under British colonisation (La Porta et al.), settler mortality and property-rights institutions (Acemoglu, John

C00556.outcome_desc: state personal income growth; tax rates, capital spending and right-to-work laws

setting.unit_desc: US state-year panel; growth analysis uses data after 1929 when state personal income estimates are available

identification.variation: within-state variation in political competition with state and year effects; IV using the 1965 Voting Rights Act in southern states
identification.threat: endogeneity of competition, likely biasing estimates downwards, and confounding with Democratic vs Republican policy differences

mechanisms.note: parties trade off utility offered to swing voters against rents captured when winning
weak competition lets incumbents capture rents and adopt anti-growth policy

settled: Chicago School argues political competition is efficient (Stigler 1972; Wittman)
contested: Whether competition between political parties has the same virtuous consequences as competition between firms
gaps: Few empirical studies speak to whether political competition matters for economic outcomes
C00556.data_asset: panel of US state policies, political competition measures and income growth
C00556.scope: US states; effect of competition on policy appears non-linear, concentrated at low competition

C00767.claim: Newspaper endorsements influence voters, who are more likely to back the endorsed candidate after publication, but influence depends on credibility: endorsements from papers biased toward that candidate's side matter less.
C00767.treatment_desc: newspaper endorsements in the 2000 and 2004 US presidential elections, varying with the paper's ideological bias
C00767.outcome_desc: individual vote choice for the endorsed candidate

Democratic vote share among readers if all papers endorsed the Democrat, 2000
Democratic vote share among readers if all papers endorsed the Democrat, 2004

setting.unit_desc: survey respondents in the 2000 and 2004 presidential campaigns

identification.variation: timing of endorsement publication relative to respondents' stated vote preference, with newspaper bias estimated from endorsement patterns
identification.threat: limited variation in the timing of endorsements across newspapers

mechanisms.note: voters rationally discount endorsements by credibility of a possibly biased informant
voters filter out media bias; endorsements are more influential among moderates and those more exposed

settled: Media exposure affects voting and turnout (DellaVigna and Kaplan 2007 on Fox News; George and Waldfogel; Gentzkow)
contested: Whether voters are unsophisticated and fail to discount media bias, or rationally filter it (Bray and Kreps 1987)
C00767.data_asset: voter survey data matched to newspaper endorsement dates and estimated newspaper bias
C00767.scope: net effect on all voters about 4% in both 2000 and 2004 assuming non-readers unaffected; larger among moderates and more exposed voters

C00570.claim: Globalization shocks, often working through culture and identity, have driven support for right-wing populism; a framework gives four channels (two demand-side, two supply-side) and reviews trade, financial and immigration evidence.

C00570.outcome_desc: support for populist (mainly right-wing) parties and candidates, e.g. the 2016 switch to Trump

setting.unit_desc: literature review plus an empirical analysis of the 2016 US presidential election

identification.variation: review of studies using shift-share and China-shock instruments, quasi-random refugee allocation and OLS correlations

mechanisms.note: identity and cultural channels matter alongside economic ones for demand for populism

settled: Standard trade theory predicts sharp redistributive effects of free trade, and past peaks of globalization saw populist backlash
contested: Whether trade shocks act directly on political preferences or through cultural channels (Autor et al. 2020 is agnostic)
Whether the China trade shock raises far-right voting: small, insignificant effects in some studies (Caselli et al. 2021 for Italy after 2008)
gaps: Mechanisms through which globalization fuels populism, requiring a fully fleshed-out political economy model
How trade, finance and labour flows each work through the political system
Why globalization, rather than other economic shocks, generates populist backlash

C00353.claim: Ethnicity enforces membership in coalitions that compete for resources: in ethnically homogeneous societies defection from losing coalitions is cheap, which rules out conflict as an equilibrium.
C00353.treatment_desc: ethnic distance, group size, income inequality and share of expropriable resources in a model of ethnic coalitions

setting.unit_desc: theoretical model with two ethnic groups; illustrated with historical episodes

mechanisms.note: conflict is a contest over expropriable assets; ethnicity limits spoils dissipation by excluding defectors
conflict can be pre-emptive when the larger group cannot rely on the smaller group committing to peace

gaps: Institutions that let groups commit to no conflict, which would remove pre-emptive ethnic conflict
C00353.scope: conflict arises for relatively low ethnic distance cost and high resource abundance; economic development removes incentives for conflict in the model

C00357.claim: Philippine municipalities barely eligible for the KALAHI-CIDSS development program, assigned by a poverty-rank threshold, suffered a large increase in conflict casualties, driven by insurgent-initiated incidents early in the programme.
C00357.treatment_desc: eligibility for the World Bank-financed community-driven development program KALAHI-CIDSS, assigned at an arbitrary poverty-rank threshold
C00357.outcome_desc: casualties in armed civil conflict, split by who initiated the incident

setting.unit_desc: municipalities within six ranks of the poverty-rank eligibility threshold

identification.variation: arbitrary poverty threshold assigning eligibility to the programme
identification.threat: eligibility alone raised violence even where municipalities did not participate, violating the IV exclusion restriction, so reduced-form RD estimates are reported; misreporting of casualties

mechanisms.note: consistent with insurgents seizing resources by force or sabotaging a programme that would weaken their support; the two are not separated

settled: Good rainfall and favourable world prices reduce conflict (Miguel et al. 2004; Dube and Vargas 2011)
contested: How development aid affects conflict: reductions in Iraq (Berman et al.; Iyengar et al.), no effect on attacks in Afghanistan (Beath et al.), increases from US food aid (Nunn and Qian)
gaps: Whether the conflict-increasing effect of aid lasts beyond the early, short-term stage of the programme
C00357.data_asset: municipality-level conflict casualties from armed forces reports matched to programme eligibility ranks
C00357.scope: identified at the eligibility margin; effect strongest during the early social preparation phase; most casualties were government troops and civilians

C00824.claim: In close Brazilian mayoral races, women mayors deliver better health outcomes, receive more discretionary transfers, are less corrupt and hire fewer temporary workers, but are less likely to be re-elected.

C00824.outcome_desc: corruption; temporary public hiring; health outcomes; federal discretionary transfers; re-election

probability of being re-elected for women elected in mixed-gender contests
share of pregnant women without prenatal visits

identification.threat: manipulation of the margin of victory, checked with a density continuity test and a falsification test on automatic FPM transfers

contested: Whether women's policy impact differs between quota-based selection and open contested elections

Whether quotas that restrict cross-gender competition differ in implications from policies that raise female participation

How people judge the thoughts and actions of others from different societies and cultures, and why social norms emerge

C00902.claim: A rational legislature organizes informative committees so that members are motivated to specialise and share information, in an incomplete-information game; committee structure follows from informational efficiency.

committee information transmission to the floor under incomplete information

C00502.claim: After New Jersey police unions lose final-offer arbitration, arrests and sentence length fall and reported crime rises relative to wins, more so the further the award is from the demand: reference points matter.

monthly property crimes per 100,000 capita in postarbitration months in Employer
elasticity of crime with respect to clearances

C00244.claim: Political selection deserves as much attention as incentives: institutions determine who enters and wins office, and pay, rents, media scrutiny and outside options shift the attractiveness of office for good versus bad types.

C00244.outcome_desc: competence and honesty of the political class

contested: Whether higher politician pay improves selection, which depends on whether public service motivation or rents dominate the draw to office
gaps: Why parties ever field bad candidates

C00961.claim: International financial market influence on advanced democracies is 'somewhat strong but somewhat narrow': markets respond to aggregate inflation and deficits, leaving governments room to move on spending composition and other policy.

long-term interest rates, total effect of elections

government employment
unemployment rate

C01019.claim: Upper-tail knowledge, proxied by Encyclopedie subscriber density across French cities, strongly predicts city growth after the onset of industrialization, whereas initial literacy relates to income levels but not to growth.

C02551.claim: A bias-corrected measure of the partisanship of congressional speech shows it was low and flat across 1873-2016 until the early 1990s, then rose sharply and is now far greater than in the past.

C00775.claim: In a lab public goods game, a payoff modification raises cooperation more when chosen democratically than when imposed: the effect of the fine on cooperation is 40 percent larger if imposed democratically.

C00203.claim: With appropriation in canonical trade models, positive shocks to labour-intensive industries reduce conflict while positive shocks to capital-intensive industries increase it; conflict must be more labour intensive than the economy.

NREGA wages provided, rupees per capita, per 1 SD improvement in bureaucratic re

C01014.outcome_desc: overall and drug-related homicides and drug (cocaine) seizures at the municipality level; also change in the mayor's party and opinions

setting.unit_desc: Mexican municipalities, 1998-2003, 2007-2010 and 1998-2013 windows

identification.variation: predicted municipal increases in international competition (strong first stage) induce manufacturing job loss

mechanisms.note: Becker-style opportunity cost: job loss lowers the opportunity cost of criminal employment, more so where criminal organizations cut illicit job-search costs and the drug trade raises returns

settled: Conflict over drug trafficking has made Mexico an epicentre of global violence, the world's second deadliest conflict zone in 2016
gaps: Violence in developing economies beyond rural areas, where the literature has traditionally focused
C01014.data_asset: Mexican municipal manufacturing employment, homicides (drug-related classification) and drug seizures matched to predicted exposure to Chinese competition
C01014.scope: concentrated in municipalities with transnational criminal organizations and where unemployment hits low-skilled men; no effect on violence in the quarter of the sample with no initial drug trade; no effect on mayoral party change

contested: Whether law merely prices behaviour or also expresses and shapes societal values, a spectrum from pure consequentialists to pure expressivists
