C02162.treatment_desc: wars fought between 1816 and 1913, financed by taxes or, given exogenous access to international credit, by external loans
C02162.outcome_desc: long-run fiscal capacity proxied by average personal income tax to GDP in 1995-2005, and a second outcome emphasising capacity rather than willingness to tax; also power-sharing institutions

setting.unit_desc: sovereign states, with wars of 1816-1913 mapped onto current state boundaries and fiscal capacity circa 2000

identification.variation: wars of 1816-1913 and their legacies for fiscal capacity circa 2000, interacted with exogenous access to international credit that allowed external war finance
identification.threat: the post-World War I boom in welfare spending makes the effect of war on fiscal capacity hard to isolate, so the wars studied end in 1913

mechanisms.note: tax-financed war builds the capacity to assess wealth and monitor compliance, while foreign loans avoid building a tax apparatus
power-sharing institutions adopted under tax-financed war protect taxpayers from arbitrary expropriation and carry the fiscal effect of war into the long run

settled: War gives rulers incentives to invest in state making and reduces domestic resistance to taxation, clearing the path to fiscal centralisation and professional tax administration
contested: Whether war always builds fiscal capacity, given that war financed by foreign loans did not when borrowers defaulted
Why rulers would not always finance war with taxes if taxation is as beneficial in the long run as earlier work suggests
C02162.data_asset: war data from 1816 mapped onto current state boundaries, external capital stocks by country, London banking crises and stock crashes, and personal income tax to GDP for 1995-2005
C02162.scope: wars of 1816-1913 and fiscal capacity circa 2000; nineteenth-century globalisation of capital markets undermined the association between war, state making and political reform

C02075.claim: Tests of congressional committee composition theories are often problematic (presumed normality and cardinality of the data); the paper's tests find little evidence of a general tendency for Democrats to stack committees.
C02075.treatment_desc: composition of congressional committees relative to the chamber, as tested by competing committee composition hypotheses, by party
C02075.outcome_desc: who sits on congressional committees: whether committee membership departs from the chamber, tested by committee and interest-group pair for Democrats and for Republicans

setting.unit_desc: US congressional committees, with committee-interest group pairs tested separately for each party

identification.variation: hypothesis tests of whether committee membership departs from the chamber, by committee-interest group pair and party, with a null hypothesis about medians
identification.threat: existing tests presume normality of the data and cardinality of the measures

contested: Whether congressional committee composition hypotheses hold, since standard tests are problematic given presumed normality and cardinality of the data

C01361.claim: With a corruptible agent, conditioning a proxy means test on more indicators can worsen targeting; in India's BPL card allocation, rule violations make the de facto allocation far less progressive than the de jure one.
C01361.treatment_desc: design of the eligibility rule for social assistance: a proxy means test conditioning on more poverty indicators, when a corruptible agent implements it, applied to Below Poverty Line cards in India
C01361.outcome_desc: progressivity and accuracy of targeting of BPL cards: card ownership by eligibility and income, bribes and prices paid, and misclassification

magnitudes.outcome: percent of ineligible households holding BPL cards
percent of eligible households without BPL cards
percent of sample households misclassified
mean implied monthly subsidy of a BPL household, in rupees

setting.unit_desc: households in a survey of Below Poverty Line card allocation in India

identification.variation: a formal model of a proxy means test with a corruptible implementing agent, with a household survey testing necessary conditions of the accuracy-enforceability tradeoff

mechanisms.note: a corruptible implementing agent makes enforceability constrain how many indicators a rule can usefully condition on
less eligible households pay larger bribes and are less likely to obtain cards, while widespread rule violations shape the de facto allocation

settled: Optimal proxy means tests can be designed by applying statistical decision theory to household survey data
contested: Whether conditioning on more poverty indicators always improves targeting, since with a corruptible agent it can worsen it through an accuracy-enforceability tradeoff
gaps: Direct tests of the accuracy-enforceability tradeoff, since the paper tests only necessary conditions for it
C01361.data_asset: household survey on BPL card ownership, bribes, rule violations and implied Fair Price Shop subsidies in India
C01361.scope: BPL card allocation in India, where households are unfamiliar with eligibility rules and official rules are frequently violated; each additional violation lowers the chance of a card by about the same amount

C01578.claim: Gifts are structured by three co-existing moral principles of economic relations, communism, exchange and hierarchy, which ordinary people combine in every society, while dominant economic forms elevate one above the others.
C01578.treatment_desc: the moral principles underlying economic relations: everyday communism, exchange or reciprocity, and hierarchy; conceptual, with no estimated treatment
C01578.outcome_desc: the moral grounds of economic transactions such as gifts and debt; no empirical outcome

identification.variation: conceptual and ethnographic argument building on Mauss's account of the gift

settled: Mauss showed that dominant economic forms, such as capitalist markets or the heroic gift, often elevate one moral principle above the others
contested: Whether the gift is a uniform economic category, which the paper denies by distinguishing co-existing moral principles
gaps: A theory of the gift that separates its co-existing moral principles, since the concept is under-theorised despite a vast literature
C01578.scope: claims that the three principles co-exist in all societies; ethnography allows us to imagine societies with a different balance of economic principles

C02501.claim: Old Bailey trials for violent and nonviolent offences, semantically indistinguishable in the late 18th century, grew steadily more distinct, driven by gradual cultural change rather than any specific legislative or bureaucratic change.
C02501.treatment_desc: evolving social attitudes toward violence, set against legislative and bureaucratic change, as drivers of how trials of violent and nonviolent offences are framed
C02501.outcome_desc: semantic distinction between violent and nonviolent trial genres in Old Bailey trial transcripts, an information-theoretic measure of the cultural framing of violence

setting.unit_desc: Old Bailey trial transcripts in London, with 60 offence categories, tracked from the late 18th century to 1910

identification.variation: coarse-graining spoken testimony into synonym sets and measuring, with information theory, how far violent and nonviolent trial genres diverge over time against a null-class model

mechanisms.note: the cultural framing of violence changed gradually through evolving social attitudes, not through particular legislative or bureaucratic change

settled: The civilizing process accompanied the state's growing monopoly of violence and the decreasing acceptability of interpersonal violence in normal social relations
contested: Whether the cultural framing of violence changed through specific legislative or bureaucratic reforms or through gradual shifts in social attitudes, which the paper favours
C02501.data_asset: large-scale Old Bailey trial transcripts, coded into synonym sets and 60 offence categories
C02501.scope: London's Old Bailey; distinct violent and nonviolent genres emerge around 1780 and the distinction keeps growing; changing victim strategies, lower tolerance of milder violence and bureaucratic vocabulary each contribute

C02004.claim: Industries with differentiated products are split by firm: large export-capable firms back reciprocal liberalization even in import-competing industries; full differentiation raises the chance of industry support by 19.3 points.
C02004.treatment_desc: degree of product differentiation in an industry, with firm heterogeneity in export potential, as the basis of firms' support for reciprocal trade liberalization
C02004.outcome_desc: industry and firm public support for or opposition to US trade agreements, and lobbying by firms and associations, coded per agreement or agreement cluster

magnitudes.outcome: chance that a net-importing industry supports an agreement, moving from a homoge
chance that a net-importing industry supports an agreement, same move, in the KO

setting.unit_desc: industries and firms taking public positions or lobbying on US trade agreements, including KORUS and AUSFTA

identification.variation: cross-industry differences in product differentiation and competitiveness, regressed on industry support and lobbying positions across trade agreements
identification.threat: conditions behind horizontal FDI, such as proprietary technology, firm competitiveness and product differentiation, could operate instead of the proposed mechanism

mechanisms.note: strong public support and lobbying for liberalization comes from large export-capable firms even in import-competing industries

settled: In US trade-agreement politics, labour unions and progressive alliances oppose trade while large corporations and multinationals support it
contested: Whether trade pits competitive against uncompetitive industries or abundant against scarce factors, or instead divides industries internally by firm
C02004.data_asset: original coding of industry and firm support, opposition and lobbying across US trade agreements, with lobbying records from the Center for Responsive Politics
C02004.scope: industries producing differentiated products; smaller firms may oppose, as in KORUS, but many remain indifferent; smaller trade partners and imperfect substitutability buffer the effect of liberalization

C00394.claim: Survey: referendum approval of new spending or debt uniformly lowers both; the initiative lowers spending and taxes in US states and Swiss cantons but raises spending in cities, and brings policy closer to majority opinion.
C00394.treatment_desc: direct democracy: mandatory or petition referendum on spending and debt, and the citizen initiative, versus representative decision-making
C00394.outcome_desc: government spending, debt and taxes (16 referendum studies listed); also social policy conservatism and congruence of policy with majority opinion

setting.unit_desc: American states, Swiss cantons and cities, as covered by the surveyed studies

identification.variation: surveyed studies compare policy across jurisdictions with and without the initiative or referendum, plus the paper's own model of petition referendum and initiative
identification.threat: literature is thin on modern causal-inference studies; initiative effects work indirectly through anticipation, so cannot be measured from measures that come to a vote

mechanisms.note: policies are more congruent with majority opinion in initiative states, suggesting the majority counteracts special interests

settled: Requiring voter approval for new spending or debt lowers spending and debt (uniform in referendum studies)
The initiative is consistently associated with more conservative social policies
Policy is more congruent with majority opinion in initiative states than in states without the initiative
contested: Whether the initiative raises or lowers spending: lower in US states and Swiss cantons but higher in cities
How far the literature identifies causal effects, given few studies use modern causal-inference methods
gaps: What makes government officials' and citizens' preferences diverge, and why they diverge the same way at the same time across jurisdictions
How often the initiative and referendum yield majoritarian policy where it ought to prevail versus where it ought to be blocked
More studies of initiative and referendum effects using modern methods of causal inference
C00394.scope: referendum effect on spending and debt is uniform; initiative effect on spending changes sign between states/cantons and cities, and depends on the relative ideal points of the key actors

C02562.claim: Emigration to the US, instrumented by frost shocks and travel costs, raised labor-movement membership, strikes, turnout and left voting in Swedish municipalities, plus welfare spending and adoption of representative democracy.
C02562.treatment_desc: total emigration from Swedish municipalities to the US over about 50 years, instrumented by 1864-67 growing-season frost shocks interacted with travel cost
C02562.outcome_desc: labor-movement membership rate 1900-1920 and strike participation; turnout and Social Democratic/left vote share in 1911-1921 national elections; per capita welfare expenditure 1918; municipal adoption of representative democracy 1919-1938

setting.unit_desc: Swedish municipalities (county-level harvest grades for the frost first stage)

identification.variation: severe local frost shocks that sparked an initial emigration wave, interacted with within-country travel costs, predict emigration over decades
identification.threat: frost shocks interacted with travel cost may violate exclusion, e.g. via proximity to trade ports and towns; addressed with hub controls, a placebo non-growing-season instrument and Conley-Hansen-Rossi bounds

mechanisms.note: results consistent with elites changing institutions to commit to better outcomes for citizens (Acemoglu and Robinson 2000, 2006)
migrant networks improved outside options of labor activists who faced elite repression for organizing

settled: Emigration to more democratic countries has positive effects on democratization and political participation at origin (Spilimbergo 2009; Docquier et al. 2016; Mercier 2016; Chauvet and Mercier 2014)
Early movers spurred further emigrants through social and family ties, producing long-lasting chain migration (Hatton and Williamson 1998)
contested: Whether emigration inhibits the use of political voice or instead raises demand for political change
C02562.data_asset: detailed Swedish municipal data 1860-1920 on emigration, labor organization, strikes, elections, welfare expenditure and local institutions, with county harvest grades 1860-1880
C02562.scope: identified from emigration driven by frost shocks and travel costs in a then-undemocratic Sweden; effects are long-run (50-year emigration) and tied to the labor movement and the political left

C01737.claim: In an RD on over 3,200 partisan sheriff elections, Democratic and Republican sheriffs comply with federal immigration detainer requests at nearly the same rate; sheriffs' views differ less across parties than the public's.
C01737.treatment_desc: electing a Democratic rather than Republican county sheriff, at a 50-50 vote tie in partisan sheriff elections
C01737.outcome_desc: sheriff compliance rate with federal requests to detain unauthorized immigrants (detainer compliance, 0-1); also 287(g) participation, jail-bed contracts, alerting ICE, background checks run

setting.unit_desc: county sheriffs; dataset of over 3,200 partisan sheriff elections, with the Table 4 compliance sample at 45 counties and 91 candidates

identification.variation: Democrat versus Republican winning close sheriff elections, compared at the 50-50 vote threshold

mechanisms.note: party of the winner matters little because candidate entry and selection make sheriffs' views similar across parties

settled: Republican and Democratic representatives make different policy choices across many offices, even with the same constituents (Lee, Moretti and Butler 2004; Besley and Case 2003)
contested: Whether elected local law-enforcement officials apply the law along partisan lines or act as neutral arbiters
Whether similar policies under Democratic and Republican local executives are an exception or reflect the constraints executives face (Ferreira and Gyourko 2009; Gerber and Hopkins 2011)
C01737.data_asset: new dataset of over 3,200 partisan sheriff elections matched to administrative data on sheriff behaviour on immigration detainer requests
C01737.scope: local to close sheriff elections where sheriffs have broad discretion; sheriffs of both parties hold more similar immigration-enforcement views than the general public

C00189.claim: Model: misperceived good actions start conflict spirals that contain the seeds of their own dissolution, since Bayesian agents eventually infer the spiral began by mistake and experiment with a good action, restarting the cycle.
C00189.treatment_desc: misperception of good actions as bad, with limited information about past actions, in sequential coordination games between two groups
C00189.outcome_desc: model prediction for the onset, duration and recurrence of inter-group conflict spirals; no empirical estimate

setting.unit_desc: overlapping generations of agents from two groups

identification.variation: overlapping-generations model in which agents of two groups play coordination games under incomplete information about whether the other side is a bad type who always takes bad actions

mechanisms.note: conflict arises from fear and distrust: each side expects bad actions and misreads good ones, as in the Hobbesian spiral view

settled: Inter-group conflict is pervasive despite mutual benefits from trust and cooperation
Conflict can stem from fear and distrust, with each side seeing war as inevitable and unwilling to cede the first-mover advantage (Thucydides)
C00189.scope: spirals require uncertainty about who started the conflict, which persists even when groups observe signals about a series of past actions; results hold while each potential conflict remains a coordination game

C02700.claim: In 900+ FCC lobbying contacts on 101 issues, large firms' amount and organisation of lobbying fit transaction-cost and collective-action predictions; small firms' do not, though they lobby less when proprietary information is at risk.
C02700.treatment_desc: collective-action problems, transaction costs (proprietary information at risk, weak appropriability) and organizational form of lobbying, by firm size
C02700.outcome_desc: number of lobbying contacts by a firm at the FCC, and whether lobbying is done individually or collectively through trade associations, separately for large and small firms

magnitudes.outcome: FCC lobbying per 1pp rise in weak appropriability (large firms, model 10)

setting.unit_desc: firm lobbying contacts at the Federal Communications Commission: over 900 contacts covering 101 issues in early 1998

identification.variation: cross-sectional variation across firms and issues in collective-action and transaction-cost characteristics, in negative-binomial count models fitted separately for large and small firms
identification.threat: organizational form may itself affect the amount of lobbying, so the two are interrelated; handled with Hausman specification tests

mechanisms.note: large-firm lobbying matches the main results of collective-action theory; small firms show little sensitivity to collective-action issues

settled: Less lobbying occurs when there are collective-action problems, the one conclusion the literature supports (Olson 1965)
Firms use nonmarket strategies such as lobbying, litigation and campaign contributions to create shareholder value (Baron 1996; Spulber 1994)
contested: Whether the organizational form of lobbying affects the amount of lobbying: the evidence is mixed at the 95% level
Whether collective-action and transaction-cost theories explain small firms' lobbying, which the paper finds they largely do not
gaps: How firms choose to organize lobbying, individually or collectively, which lobbying theory has largely omitted in favour of the amount of lobbying
C02700.data_asset: new dataset of over 900 lobbying contacts covering 101 issues at the Federal Communications Commission in early 1998
C02700.scope: large firms behave as theory predicts and small firms do not; one agency (FCC) in early 1998; small firms lobby less when they must reveal proprietary information

C02169.claim: Overview of EU-28 labor-market reforms since the 2008/09 crisis (dismissal protection, unemployment benefits, ALMPs) asking whether they made labor markets less dualized; the slices give no verdict.
C02169.treatment_desc: EU-28 labor-market reforms after 2008/09: employment protection (dismissal protection, limits on fixed-term contracts), unemployment benefit generosity and coverage, and intensity of active labor market policies
C02169.outcome_desc: labor-market dualization between secure and insecure jobs: dismissal protection, provision of unemployment benefits and access to ALMPs; hirings on temporary contracts

setting.unit_desc: EU-28 countries

identification.variation: descriptive overview of reform patterns across EU-28 countries, with some evidence on changes in hirings on temporary contracts

settled: Labor-market segmentation, a divide between secure and insecure jobs, is related to problems of macro-economic efficiency, workers' well-being and social cohesion

C02481.claim: Relatives of Philippine office-holders get better-paid jobs: in an RD on close 2007 elections, managerial employment rises 0.48pp (over 19% of the control mean); the effect is 45% lower for women.
C02481.treatment_desc: being related to a current office-holder (a candidate who narrowly won rather than narrowly lost a municipal election), with family links identified from naming conventions
C02481.outcome_desc: probability of being employed in better-paying occupations, especially managerial positions, among relatives of candidates (nepotism and favoritism in employment)

magnitudes.outcome: managerial employment of relatives of office-holders
managerial employment vs control mean (stated as more than 19%)

setting.unit_desc: individuals in an administrative dataset of 20 million people, linked to candidates in the 2007 and 2010 municipal elections

identification.variation: relatives of candidates who narrowly won versus narrowly lost the 2007 mayoral elections, plus a control group of individuals connected to candidates elected in 2010
identification.threat: relatives of losing candidates may bear a cost from the connection, which would inflate the RD contrast; addressed with control groups of relatives of later-elected candidates

mechanisms.note: authors caution against political decentralization in areas of weak accountability, such as most Philippine municipalities

contested: How large the value of political connections to individuals is once the cost of being related to a losing candidate is netted out
gaps: Long-term impacts of political connections on occupations; the data only allow the short-term value
Whether political favoritism in employment affects the local delivery of public services
C02481.data_asset: administrative dataset collected in 2008-2010 on 20 million individuals in the Philippines, linked to 2007 and 2010 election candidates through naming conventions
C02481.scope: identified at close 2007 mayoral elections; effect appears throughout the occupational distribution but is largest at the top, and short-term only

C01802.claim: Model: democracy is sustainable when opposing politicians are neither very attractive nor very unattractive; backsliding occurs when citizens knowingly consent to a highly appealing incumbent or unconditionally oppose him.
C01802.treatment_desc: attractiveness of the incumbent relative to opposing politicians, and citizens' valuation of their future ability to replace the government
C01802.outcome_desc: model prediction of whether democracy is sustained or erodes through incumbent backsliding; no empirical estimate

identification.variation: dynamic model in which an incumbent takes steps that reduce citizens' ability to remove him and citizens weigh satisfaction with him against their future ability to replace him

mechanisms.note: electoral discipline erodes when citizens let appealing incumbents gain security, or when incumbents who are unconditionally opposed stay only by backsliding

settled: Most backsliding governments find ways to remain in power, recovering from temporary electoral reversals (e.g. AKP, PiS, Fidesz)
contested: Why citizens do not react in time to gradual backsliding steps that will harm them
C01802.scope: conditions in a stylised dynamic model; the conclusion illustrates them informally with Turkey, Poland, Hungary and Venezuela

C00695.claim: A randomised community-driven reconstruction program in post-conflict Liberia raised cooperation in a matching-funds game only where men and women faced the problem together, via better mobilization; none in all-women communities.
C00695.treatment_desc: random assignment of a donor-funded community-driven reconstruction (CDR) program that created community development councils, run with the International Rescue Committee
C00695.outcome_desc: contributions in a matching-funds public-goods game (cooperation capacity), plus mobilization activity, trust in leaders and use of democratic process, in mixed-gender versus all-women communities

setting.unit_desc: post-conflict communities in a field experiment (Lofa County field team)

identification.variation: random assignment of the CDR program across communities, with randomised matching-funds game treatments and gender composition of game participants set by design

mechanisms.note: program effects worked through improved mobilization capacity that may have helped coordinate mixed-gender problems, not through leader trust

settled: Social cooperation is critical to a wide variety of political and economic outcomes
Use of democratic procedures independently raises cooperation in public-goods games (Dal Bo, Foster and Putterman 2010)
contested: Whether cooperative capacity is a stable, historically rooted trait of a political unit or can respond to short-term interventions
C00695.data_asset: matching-funds game and follow-up community surveys collected in randomised Liberian communities by the authors' field teams with the IRC
C00695.scope: effects appear only in communities where both men and women took part in the matching-funds game, by design; none where only women took part; post-conflict Liberia

C01820.claim: Model: an autocrat holds fair elections to signal his popularity; more elite repression of the opposition makes fair elections less likely, while a higher cost of protesting for ordinary citizens makes them more likely.
C01820.treatment_desc: elite repression of opposition leaders and the cost to ordinary citizens of protesting (cruelty toward common people)
C01820.outcome_desc: model prediction of the probability that a non-democratic incumbent allows free and fair elections; the appendix reports regressions of free elections on repression and cruelty across non-democracies

setting.unit_desc: theory; Appendix B checks predictions on non-democratic countries (linear probability models, with logit and non-OECD robustness)

identification.variation: signalling model: an informed incumbent chooses fair or farcical elections, then heterogeneous citizens vote and decide whether to protest, more willing if others protest

mechanisms.note: fair elections serve as a signal of the incumbent's popularity to citizens, who cannot tell if a missing challenger was blocked or deterred
citizens protest more willingly if they expect others to protest, so regime cruelty toward protesters shapes the signalling choice

settled: Elections are common in non-democracies, from farces with near-100% incumbent vote to contests with opposition candidates and international observers
A substantial political-science literature explains elections held by autocrats (Gandhi and Lust-Okar 2009; Miller 2015; Gehlbach et al. 2016)
contested: How elite repression and the cost of protest shape an autocrat's choice of fair elections; the equilibrium comparative statics differ from those in the existing theories
gaps: When during the incumbent's tenure free elections should be held, as a dynamic problem; the model's incumbent-opposition interaction is one-shot
How opposition leaders compete, participate and coordinate on one candidate in the shadow of an authoritarian incumbent
Why incumbents call unscheduled elections and why oppositions campaign or boycott
C01820.scope: unique equilibrium with intuitive comparative statics; repression has a persistent effect since past repressiveness makes new repression more effective; interaction is one-shot

C01792.skip_reason: wrong PDF: slices are a theory paper on partisan factions, dissent and over-reform within an accountability framework (cites work up to 2024), not Ashworth and Shotts (2010) on informative media commentary and pandering

C02535.claim: Compared with the rest of the world, Latin American inequality was not high in pre-conquest 1491, in the post-conquest decades, or even in the mid-19th century, contrary to the view that early inequality supported rent-seeking institutions.
C02535.treatment_desc: Iberian conquest of the Americas after 1491-92 and the claim that it created very high inequality early on
C02535.outcome_desc: Gini coefficient of income inequality in Latin America from 1491 onward, predicted from a pre-industrial Gini regression and compared with the rest of the world

magnitudes.outcome: predicted Latin American Gini before the Iberians arrived (1491)
Gini per 1pp rise in urbanization rate, pre-industrial regression

setting.unit_desc: Latin America as a region over five centuries from 1491, benchmarked against pre-industrial societies elsewhere

identification.variation: Gini regression fitted on pre-industrial societies (income per capita, urbanization, density) used to predict Latin American Ginis, compared with the rest of the world and with backward-projected pseudo-Ginis

contested: Whether high inequality arose early after the conquest and supported rent-seeking, anti-growth institutions, as most analysts believe (the paper argues it did not)
C02535.data_asset: ancient and pre-industrial Gini estimates plotted against GDP per capita, with Latin American population-density and urbanization estimates and backward-projected pseudo-Ginis (Prados de la Escosura 2007)
C02535.scope: inequality is reconstructed from a pre-industrial Gini regression and benchmarks, not measured directly; the comparison is with the rest of the world

C02623.claim: Model: average-cost pricing, with no transfers to the regulated firm, can dominate marginal-cost pricing when regulators may identify with the industry, giving a rationale for the observed prohibition of transfers.
C02623.treatment_desc: restrictions on regulators' instruments and scope: average-cost pricing (no transfers) versus marginal-cost pricing (transfers allowed), with regulatory hearings giving watchdogs a say
C02623.outcome_desc: model prediction of social welfare and of which regulatory mandate is optimal for a natural monopoly; no empirical estimate

setting.unit_desc: regulation of a natural monopoly (stylised model)

identification.variation: stylised model in which a regulator with private information may collude with the industry and watchdog groups can alter rule making; two mandates compared behind a veil of ignorance

mechanisms.note: regulator with discretion and private information may collude with the industry; mandate design trades regulatory flexibility against counter-powers
regulators may identify with interest groups, and watchdog advocacy groups can alter proposed rules at hearings

settled: Transfers to the regulated firm are prohibited in some industries, while much theory assumes a benevolent regulator barred from transfers subject to the firm's budget constraint
contested: Whether prohibiting transfers can be rationalised: it conflicts with assuming a benevolent regulator, and either mandate can be optimal depending on parameters
Whether transfers are less likely to be prohibited when public decision makers are less prone to collude with the regulated industry
gaps: Constitutional design of regulatory institutions by self-interested framers rather than by a social planner behind the veil of ignorance
A positive theory of regime choice, feeding consumer, industry, taxpayer and agency lobbying into a model of congressional voting and political pressure
C02623.scope: very stylised model of natural-monopoly regulation with framers behind a veil of ignorance; not meant to support prohibiting transfers, only to show what makes such prohibitions more likely

C00173.claim: General framework for institutional dynamics under stochastic shifts in payoffs and political power: with ordered states and single-crossing conditions a Markov voting equilibrium exists; applied to repression and experimentation.
C00173.treatment_desc: stochastic changes in payoffs and in the distribution of political power across ordered institutional states (political rights, repression, policies)
C00173.outcome_desc: model predictions of institutional transitions, extension of political rights and repression, and collective experimentation; no empirical estimate

setting.unit_desc: general model; the Russian revolutions up to October 1917 serve as illustration

identification.variation: dynamic model with ordered states and players, single-crossing preferences and a stochastic distribution of political power; Markov voting equilibrium

mechanisms.note: generalises median-voter logic to dynamic stochastic settings where the pivotal players (quasi-median voters) change as states change

settled: Political change often takes place amid uncertainty and turmoil, sometimes bringing the most radical factions to power (Jacobins, Nazis, Bolsheviks)
gaps: Applications of the Markov voting framework beyond political economy, such as the internal politics of the firm in organizational economics
Dynamic stochastic models of regime transitions with several heterogeneous groups forming temporary coalitions and gradual enfranchisement or disenfranchisement
C00173.scope: existence needs ordered states and players plus single-crossing payoffs and power shifting in the same direction as preferences; uniqueness and comparative statics need further conditions

C02322.claim: Individuals from African ethnic groups organized in segmentary lineages show a larger gap between trust in relatives and non-relatives, because they trust non-relatives less; the effect is found mainly in rural areas.
C02322.treatment_desc: traditional segmentary-lineage organization of the individual's ethnic group, as against other forms of traditional social organization
C02322.outcome_desc: relatives trust gap (trust in relatives minus trust in non-relatives), decomposed into trust in non-relatives and trust in relatives, separately for rural and urban respondents

setting.unit_desc: individuals in sub-Saharan Africa matched to the traditional lineage organization of their ethnic group

identification.variation: ethnic groups' traditional segmentary-lineage organization compared across individuals, with the pattern contrasted between rural and urban respondents
identification.threat: estimates are OLS correlations; the rural-only pattern is the support offered for a causal reading

mechanisms.note: traditional social structure persists in rural areas and shrinks associational life beyond kin, lowering trust of non-relatives

settled: Economies are embedded in societies: a large number of complementary social norms must exist for an economic system to work and cannot be taken for granted
gaps: Stronger causal evidence on how traditional lineage organization shapes the scope of trust; the paper calls its evidence preliminary
C02322.scope: gap arises from lower trust in non-relatives, not higher trust in relatives; rural point estimates are 4-10 times those for urban respondents; sub-Saharan Africa only

C01646.claim: In four pre-registered dictator-game experiments (N = 3591), thinking about karma or God reduced selfishness among believers, not non-believers, moving initially selfish offers toward fairness and leaving fair offers unchanged.
C01646.treatment_desc: randomised priming of thoughts about karma or God before an anonymous dictator game, with belief in karma or God as moderator
C01646.outcome_desc: amount offered to an anonymous recipient in a dictator game (selfishness versus fair offers), by believers and non-believers

setting.unit_desc: participants across four experiments (Hindus, Buddhists, Christians and non-religious Americans among them)

identification.variation: random assignment to a karma, God or control frame before dictator-game giving, with belief in karma or God as moderator
identification.threat: effects might reflect acquiescence to a shared intuition or primed ideas about fairness, which believers and non-believers both link to karma

mechanisms.note: norm adherence rises when believers think of supernatural forces, but is not moderated by punitive or benevolent views or by social learning of the belief

settled: Commitment to moralizing gods goes with adherence to norms of cooperation, honesty and generosity toward strangers across cultures (Purzycki et al. 2016; Shariff and Norenzayan 2011)
Religious reminders have no reliable effect on non-believers (meta-analyses: Shariff et al. 2016; Willard et al. 2016)
contested: Whether supernatural punishment or supernatural benevolence drives believers' prosocial behaviour, and whether signalling to others explains framing effects
gaps: Whether supernatural framing shifts behaviour when the normative response is not a fair split, such as giving the whole endowment to a clearly needy recipient
Whether the results generalise to broader human cultural and religious diversity beyond these samples
What mechanism supports supernatural framing effects, and whether it differs between God and karma or across religious groups

C01151.outcome_desc: probability that a rural public clinic has a doctor assigned (filled post); secondary: doctor attendance at unannounced visits, and doctors reporting direct connections to politicians

magnitudes.outcome: doctors reporting direct connections with politicians, governing-party vs other

setting.unit_desc: 850 rural public clinics in Punjab (34% of 2,496) surveyed three times in 2011-12; RD estimates use subsets within bandwidths; 2002 and 2008 election data

identification.variation: close PML(N) wins versus losses in 2008 provincial assembly races, plus a geographic RD on clinics' distance to the constituency boundary
identification.threat: few close elections involving the governing party make estimates imprecise; sorting around the cutoff and winners' ability to win systematically (tested, none found); 1 km geographic RD may be a LATE for outlying areas

mechanisms.note: speculative: government doctor jobs as a divisible benefit to supporters, with doctors acting as local political interlocutors
politicians routinely interfere in the health department to shield shirking doctors from sanctions; about 32% of officers report pressure from assembly members

settled: Political connections are valuable: those with access to elected officials receive more favours and services (Albouy 2013; Ansolabehere and Snyder 2006; Brollo and Nannicini 2012; Fisman 2001)
Public worker absence is a key obstacle to delivering services to the poor in developing countries (Chaudhury et al. 2006)
contested: Whether voters who elect governing-party politicians are better off overall, since more services may be offset by a policy mix with more non-programmatic spending and lower quality
Whether the net welfare effect of political alignment is positive, given that the paper can only document potential costs alongside the known benefits
gaps: Net welfare effect of alignment: how many new areas are served, whether the service is transferable, effects on extent and quality, and whether service is targeted at the expense of general welfare
Whether doctors in governing-party areas target services to politically defined subsets such as swing voters
Direct effect of politicians' interference on bureaucratic outcomes, unmeasurable here because bureaucratic areas intersect constituencies unevenly
C01151.data_asset: first representative panel survey of 850 rural public clinics (unannounced visits), geo-referenced clinic and constituency boundaries, 2002 and 2008 Punjab election results, survey of senior health bureaucrats
C01151.scope: Identified at close governing-party wins and constituency boundaries in Punjab; attendance estimates are imprecise and sometimes negative; costs arise where service quality matters, not for one-off goods such as roads.

C01140.claim: Meeting the school-quality target cut Brazilian mayors' re-election probability by 8.5pp (RD); a field experiment informing voters of school quality also lowered incumbent support, except among parents of municipal-school pupils.
C01140.treatment_desc: positive signal of municipal school quality: barely meeting vs missing the federal IDEB target (RD across Brazilian municipalities), and a field experiment giving Pernambuco voters information on local school quality
C01140.outcome_desc: probability that the incumbent mayor is re-elected (RD, municipalities near the IDEB target); incumbent vote choice in the field experiment

magnitudes.outcome: incumbent mayor re-election probability, meeting the IDEB target (preferred loca
same effect, share of a standard deviation (paper: over 17%)

setting.unit_desc: municipality-election observations within the 0.388 bandwidth of the IDEB target (Table 1 preferred column); field experiment with a random sample of voters in Pernambuco; online survey experiment with a diverse sample of Brazilian voters

identification.variation: municipalities that barely met versus barely missed their IDEB school-quality target, complemented by randomised provision of school-quality information to voters in Pernambuco
identification.threat: dependence on bandwidth choice (estimates stable but some confidence intervals cross 0); the field experiment addresses internal validity and heterogeneity; the online survey mechanism evidence is suggestive, not conclusive

mechanisms.note: voters who prioritise education update on mayors' type as political agency models predict; low-priority voters read school quality as misplaced priorities and perceive trade-offs with social assistanc

settled: Information provision often fails to produce performance-based accountability voting in the electorate at large (Dunning et al. 2019a, 2019b; Boas, Hidalgo and Melo 2019)
Poor voters in Brazil disapprove of increased educational spending because they prefer cash transfers (Bursztyn 2016)
contested: Whether information on public service quality prompts accountability voting for the whole electorate or only for subgroups or under specific conditions (Adida et al. 2017, 2020; Boas and Hidalgo 2019)
Whether electoral accountability sometimes works in undesirable directions, with voters punishing good performers and rewarding bad ones (Adida et al. 2020; Arias et al. 2018; Chong et al. 2015)
gaps: Stronger causal evidence that voters infer policy-priority trade-offs from school quality, since the online survey experiment is suggestive rather than conclusive
Whether accountability interventions that account for voters' varied policy interests and boost interest representation work better
C01140.data_asset: federal IDEB school-quality targets and results matched to municipal election returns, a preregistered field experiment in Pernambuco (EGAP Metaketa) and a preregistered online survey experiment
C01140.scope: RD identified at the IDEB-target threshold; negative effect driven by voters who give low priority to education (a majority of Brazilians), while parents of children in municipal schools respond in the expected direction.

C01118.claim: Voters quasi-randomly assigned to polling stations in poor-infrastructure public schools gave Macri, the ex-mayor running for president in 2015, a 0.22pp lower vote share; larger in low-income areas and where more households have children.
C01118.treatment_desc: being assigned (by alphabetical order of surname within electoral circuits) to vote in a public school with poorer infrastructure, exposing voters to school quality minutes before voting
C01118.outcome_desc: Mauricio Macri's share of votes at the ballot-station (school precinct) level in the three 2015 Argentine presidential election rounds, City of Buenos Aires

magnitudes.outcome: Macri vote share, poor vs good infrastructure school (intro figure; conclusion s
Macri vote share in low-income circuits (paper range 0.49-0.53; lower bound show
Macri vote share in low-income circuits with many school-age children (paper ran

setting.unit_desc: 456 public schools (each hosting ballot stations) across 158 electoral circuits in the City of Buenos Aires; three election rounds Aug-Nov 2015, school infrastructure scored 2015-2016

identification.variation: within electoral circuits, voters are assigned to ballot stations in different schools by alphabetical order of last name, so exposure to good versus poor school infrastructure is quasi-random
identification.threat: surname distribution could correlate with school quality within circuits; balance checks show voters at good and bad schools are similar on age, gender, electors per booth and housing prices

mechanisms.note: direct exposure to poor school infrastructure at the time of voting makes public education and the incumbent's performance salient; not driven by information scarcity

settled: Voters often fail to turn available performance information into useful knowledge, e.g. attributing luck to effort (Healy et al. 2010) or being swayed by ballot order (Blom-Hansen et al. 2016)
Information presented more visibly and at the appropriate time has larger effects on decisions (DellaVigna 2009; Mani and Mukand 2007; Harding and Stasavage 2013)
contested: Whether voters' lapses in using available information reflect information-processing frictions or mental gaps (Handel and Schwartzstein 2018)
Whether polling-place context moves votes through unconscious behavioural confusion (Shue and Luttmer 2009) or through attention to a salient issue, as this paper argues
gaps: Individual-level voting responses to school quality, since only ballot-station aggregates and circuit-level household averages are available
Whether the salience effect holds outside the City of Buenos Aires, to which the analysis is limited by data availability
C01118.data_asset: ballot-station results from the Camara Nacional Electoral for three 2015 rounds, matched to school infrastructure scores (1-4) from the General Directorate of School Infrastructure and circuit-level household data
C01118.scope: Effect concentrated among voters with a larger stake in public schools (low-income circuits, households with school-age children); no effect on turnout or invalid votes; incumbent was the former mayor responsible for city schools.

C01186.claim: State governments give more water cisterns to copartisan-led municipalities only where the mayor's clientelistic mobilization capacity is weak; where it is strong, they favour opposition-led municipalities and avoid their strongholds.
C01186.treatment_desc: alignment of the municipality's mayor with the state governing party, interacted with the mayor's local clientelistic mobilization capacity (party membership strength)
C01186.outcome_desc: number of water cisterns allocated to a municipality by its state government (administrative data, semi-arid Brazil)

setting.unit_desc: semi-arid municipalities receiving cisterns allocated by state governments; NGO, municipal and total cistern series also used

identification.variation: state-government cistern allocation across municipalities by mayoral alignment and mobilization capacity (interaction specification), checked with a close-election RD on alignment
identification.threat: alignment of mayors with the state is not random, so an RD on close mayoral elections is used, estimating the alignment effect separately for weak- and strong-machine samples

mechanisms.note: irrevocable, durable benefits raise voters' income and weaken machines' hold, so incumbents avoid their own strong machines instead of targeting core areas as in standard clientelism

settled: Parties use targeted redistribution to create and sustain ties with voters (Golden and Min 2013)
Irrevocable, durable benefits can reduce voters' dependence on incumbents: titling in Mexico, cisterns in Brazil, grants in Uganda (Larreguy et al. 2018; Bobonis et al. 2019; Blattman et al. 2018)
contested: Whether machines should target core constituencies, as with other benefits (Diaz-Cayeros et al. 2016; Stokes et al. 2013), or opposition areas when the benefit has a lasting income effect
Whether durable benefits build loyalty through reciprocity or commitment signals, or erode machines by raising voters' reservation values
gaps: Whether durable benefits can raise electoral competition in areas dominated by monopolist machines without a shift to programmatic politics
How nondominant parties that win the central government before poor rural areas (PAN in Mexico, PT in Brazil) use such allocation strategies against entrenched machines
C01186.data_asset: previously unused administrative data on cisterns allocated by state governments, NGOs and municipalities across 1,130 semi-arid Brazilian municipalities, 2003-12, with party membership and mayoral election data
C01186.scope: Aligned municipalities gain only where mobilization capacity is weak (roughly the first 45% of the sample); federal allocation showed no political criteria; the theory predicts the strategy is likelier where benefits are more valuable.

C01219.claim: West Bengal panchayats narrowly won by the ruling party get more NREGA labour (about 1 day per household, 13%) and return 1.5-1.8pp more national votes for it; both gaps are concentrated in water-stressed areas.
C01219.treatment_desc: state ruling party (AITC) winning a bare majority on the gram panchayat council in the 2013 election (multidimensional RD), split into water-stressed (groundwater depth above median) and non-water-stressed areas
C01219.outcome_desc: per-household NREGA labour days allocated to the panchayat in the 2014-2016 dry seasons; secondary: ruling party vote share at polling stations in the 2014 national election

magnitudes.outcome: NREGA labour days per household, ruling-party vs opposition panchayats (overall
same effect as a share of the comparison mean (roughly 13%)
ruling party national vote share at polling stations in ruling-party panchayats

setting.unit_desc: gram panchayats and their polling stations in West Bengal; 11 million NREGA job cards; number of panchayats in the estimation sample not in the slices

identification.variation: multidimensional running variable built from seat-level vote shares in the 2013 council election, measuring distance from the ruling party winning an absolute council majority
identification.threat: water stress measured by a median split might proxy for something else (checked with the 8-metre well-drilling cost discontinuity); administrative frictions between officials of different parties could drive allocations (authors judge this implausible)

mechanisms.note: local officials act as frontline workers of the party machine, and NREGA jobs are channelled to co-partisan councils where scarcity makes jobs most valuable, with vote returns

settled: Politicians in India give selective access to services to prospective voters and disburse aid before elections (Cole 2009; Asher and Novosad 2017; Cole et al. 2012)
Local officials often serve as frontline workers of the political machine (Shenoy and Zimmermann 2022; Bussell 2019)
contested: Whether aid disbursed during a crisis follows need or political targeting, since aggregate patterns can look altruistic while masking favouritism by co-partisans
Whether politicians treat scarcity as a problem to prevent or as an opportunity to cement their power (Wade 1982)
gaps: Whether the competitiveness of the political environment dampens or amplifies the incentive for political targeting
Whether forward-looking politicians distort investments to keep voters vulnerable to water scarcity and grateful for aid
Which of two candidate scenarios is the true mechanism behind the targeted allocations and vote gains (scenarios not specified in the slices)
C01219.data_asset: universe of 2013 West Bengal gram panchayat results (over 100,000 candidates), 2014 polling-station results, 11 million NREGA job cards (300 million job spells) and 1,048 groundwater monitoring wells
C01219.scope: Identified at bare ruling-party council majorities in West Bengal; effects are concentrated in water-stressed areas, with no partisan differences in allocation or votes where water is not scarce.

C01191.claim: Senegalese rural communities split in 2008 got about 2,000 FCFA (~50% of baseline mean) more per capita central transfers; the signaling theory says incumbents use costly splits to reach groups lacking a history of reciprocity.
C01191.treatment_desc: creation of new administrative units by splitting Senegalese rural communities (CRs) in 2008, targeted by incumbents facing rising electoral competition (new CRs and rump CRs versus no-split CRs)
C01191.outcome_desc: per capita transfers from the national government to rural communities, 2007-2014, split versus no-split communities

magnitudes.outcome: per capita central government transfers to rural communities after a split, in F
same effect relative to the baseline mean (about 50%)

setting.unit_desc: Senegalese rural communities (CRs); a cross-country panel on contestation and administrative unit proliferation is also used; the number of CRs is not in the slices

identification.variation: 2008 CR splits (new and rump CRs) versus non-splitting CRs, comparing transfers and incumbent vote share before and after
identification.threat: anticipation effects and comparing a national (2007) with a local (2009) election; homogenisation of new CR boundaries; the Mouride brotherhood's organisational capacity (robust to dropping Mbacke department)

mechanisms.note: promises of local public goods are credible only with a history of targeting; costly new units, with stable transfers and cheaper future targeting, signal commitment to other groups
incumbents target groups with strong brokers able to coordinate votes and a history of reciprocal exchange; splits reach groups without that history

settled: Efficiency (functionalist) explanations of new administrative units are rejected in favour of political economy ones based on electoral benefits to national incumbents (Pierskalla 2016a)
Splits give incumbents patronage jobs, co-opt local elites and divide the opposition (Green 2010; Hassan 2016; Malesky 2009; Resnick 2014)
Incumbents under electoral pressure are rewarded by voters in newly created units (Grossman and Lewis 2014; Hassan 2016)
contested: Whether incumbents mainly react to bottom-up demand from marginalised or mobilised areas (Grossman and Lewis 2014; Pierskalla 2016b) or choose splits strategically as costly signals
Whether splits improve public service delivery, whose overall effect is somewhat ambiguous (Pierskalla 2016a)
gaps: Conditions that support brokers' ability to coordinate votes, beyond the scope of this paper
Factors that sustain groups' partisan bias even when parties are nonprogrammatic and nonideological
How the economic independence of brokers from the state shapes reciprocal exchange between groups and a party
C01191.data_asset: Senegalese rural community electoral results (2000-09), central transfers (2007-14) and public goods data, plus a cross-country panel of administrative units (Grossman et al. 2017) with democracy and contestation measures
C01191.scope: Theory aimed at new democracies and electoral authoritarian regimes with weak information and nonprogrammatic parties; Senegal gives incumbents close to full control over splits; cross-country link from contestation to unit proliferation depends on ethnolingui

C01152.claim: Doctors in the least competitive Punjab constituencies are 20pp less likely to be present than in the most competitive, connected doctors 17.7pp less; monitoring raised attendance only in competitive areas and for unconnected doctors.
C01152.treatment_desc: electoral competitiveness of the provincial assembly constituency a clinic sits in (most versus least competitive tercile), via a geographic RD at constituency boundaries; also doctors' connections to the local politician and a smartphone-monitoring reform
C01152.outcome_desc: probability that a doctor is present at an unannounced audit visit to a rural public clinic

magnitudes.outcome: doctor attendance, most vs least competitive tercile (paper: moving from most to
doctor attendance, doctor connected to the local politician
doctor attendance, connected doctor in the least competitive tercile
doctor attendance after smartphone-monitoring reform, most competitive tercile (

setting.unit_desc: 850 of 2,496 rural public clinics in Punjab (297 constituencies), three unannounced visits Nov 2011-Oct 2012; interviews with 34 senior health officials and 116 inspectors; RD uses subsets within bandwidths

identification.variation: geographic discontinuity in constituency competitiveness at provincial assembly boundaries that cut across health administrative boundaries; reform effects from a province-wide RCT and a dashboard-flagging RD
identification.threat: covariate imbalances at low bandwidths (slope, registered voters, turnout 2008) and possible placement of clinics by competition; sensitivity to clinics very near boundaries checked; the design cannot show exactly why competition matters

mechanisms.note: low competition marks a patronage equilibrium where doctor postings are political currency; politicians shield connected doctors from sanction (40% of senior officials report interference)
monitoring and data raise attendance only where political competition is high and for doctors unconnected to politicians, so the principal-agent fix is constrained by politics

settled: Public worker absenteeism is a persistent problem: one in three educators and one in five health workers were absent across six countries in the early 2000s (Chaudhury et al. 2006)
Government jobs are well suited to patronage and are often used for vote buying (Robinson and Verdier 2013; Xu 2018; Gans-Morse et al. 2014; Folke et al. 2011)
contested: Whether monitoring and incentive reforms reduce absenteeism, given mixed effects in the literature (Banerjee and Duflo 2006; Olken and Pande 2012; Muralidharan et al. 2019)
Whether absence is mainly an information asymmetry between principals and agents, or a political problem of patronage that blocks reform
gaps: Exactly why political competition affects doctor attendance, which the discontinuity design cannot show
Whether making inspection data public to raise voter awareness of absence would amplify political costs, since politicians objected to a public dashboard
When policymakers act on data, and whether evidence alone can improve service delivery where power is concentrated
C01152.data_asset: interviews with 34 of 36 senior health officials and 116 inspectors, a representative panel of 850 clinics with unannounced attendance audits, election outcomes and smartphone inspection dashboard data
C01152.scope: Punjab, Pakistan; reform and flagging effects are confined to competitive constituencies and doctors without political connections; geographic RD identified at constituency boundaries.

C01147.claim: Presidential incumbents did better in Brazilian municipalities that implemented the Minha Casa Minha Vida housing programme (DiD), even though lottery winners were no more likely than non-winners to support incumbents.
C01147.treatment_desc: implementation of the Minha Casa Minha Vida housing programme in a municipality (staggered rollout, DiD); direct effect of winning the housing lottery estimated separately in two surveys
C01147.outcome_desc: vote share of the incumbent presidential candidate (and mayoral incumbents) in municipalities with versus without the programme, before versus after

magnitudes.outcome: incumbent presidential vote share, MCMV x Post, all cycles combined (Table 2; vo
same, 2006-10 cycle (smallest cycle estimate)
same, 2010-14 cycle (largest cycle estimate)

setting.unit_desc: Brazilian municipalities over three presidential cycles (2006-10, 2010-14, 2014-18) and two local cycles; lottery surveys of about 3,000 applicants (2011 and 2016 lotteries, interviewed 2017 and 2020)

identification.variation: staggered rollout of MCMV across municipalities, comparing not-yet-treated municipalities at the start of each cycle; lottery assignment of beneficiaries for the direct effect
identification.threat: rollout across municipalities is not random, so the authors restrict to not-yet-treated municipalities and add a matched variant; lottery winners cannot reveal indirect effects on non-beneficiaries

mechanisms.note: the programme is conspicuous, widely known, attributed to the PT and well regarded by non-beneficiaries, who far outnumber beneficiaries
social programmes act as advertising that signals politicians' priorities and competence to the wider electorate; politicians saw MCMV as an electoral asset

settled: Policy feedback can take forms beyond direct effects on beneficiaries (Jacobs and Mettler 2018)
Direct effects of programmes are usually studied by comparing beneficiaries with similar non-beneficiaries (Campbell 2012)
contested: Whether a large, conspicuous programme earns its electoral returns from beneficiaries or mainly from the much larger group of non-beneficiaries
Whether beneficiaries reward incumbents, given a null average effect but more negative evaluations among winners with poor experiences or longer waits
gaps: Circumstances under which the electorate evaluates policies differently from direct beneficiaries, and which other feedback channels shape electoral dividends of public policy
Relative importance of feedback channels, whether they are substitutes or complements, and when politicians favour one over another
Trade-off between a programme's visibility and the quality of its implementation
C01147.data_asset: two original surveys of about 3,000 housing-lottery applicants (795 recent, 2,119 early lotteries), 15 qualitative interviews and municipal presidential and mayoral results matched to the programme rollout
C01147.scope: Programme with large, conspicuous benefits reaching a small share of the electorate; lottery winners show no direct electoral bonus, so returns come from non-beneficiaries; authors expect broad indirect returns to be harder in polarised electorates.

C00443.claim: A model with voter, politician and bureaucrat implies accountability differs by bureaucratic quality (pooling on rents at low quality, voter learning at intermediate); a meta-study of Brazilian mayor studies is congruent with it.
C00443.treatment_desc: municipal bureaucratic quality as the moderator of electoral accountability: a new measure for Brazilian municipalities used to re-examine studies of mayors' rent allocation, voter updating and incumbency disadvantage
C00443.outcome_desc: equilibrium accountability in a theory model; meta-study outcomes are the share of audited funds a mayor allocates to rents, voter feeling-thermometer updating on a clean-mayor signal, and incumbency disadvantage in mayoral elections

setting.unit_desc: Brazilian municipalities in the replicated studies (audited mayors, survey experiments, close mayoral elections); sample sizes and years not in the slices

identification.variation: two-period model of electoral accountability where a politician and an unelected bureaucrat co-produce public goods, tested through a theoretically structured meta-study of four Brazilian studies re-analysed by bureaucratic quality
identification.threat: the meta-study rests on qualitative congruence across studies with distinct samples, treatments and outcomes; omitted confounders (a confounder would need 4-9 times the predictive power of the strongest covariate to explain away estimates)

mechanisms.note: voters can learn politician competence from public goods only at intermediate and higher bureaucratic quality; at very low quality both types pool on rents
at somewhat higher quality incompetent types invest in public goods in a first term and shirk later; this arises only at low quality relative to the Brazilian sample
bureaucratic quality conditions the efficiency of politicians' public goods investments; rent allocations are predicted and found to fall with bureaucratic quality

settled: In standard accountability models voters evaluate politicians on observed public goods outcomes (Ashworth 2012)
Politicians rely on bureaucrats of widely differing quality to co-produce public goods
contested: Why electoral accountability findings are heterogeneous and mixed, including whether making public goods outcomes more visible improves accountability (Enriquez et al. 2023; Incerti 2020)
Whether accountability failures reflect uninformed or non-Bayesian voters (Dunning et al. 2019; Achen and Bartels 2016; Healy et al. 2010) or rational voters facing bureaucratic co-production
gaps: How other features of bureaucratic organisations, such as incentives, actions and outputs, condition electoral politics across contexts
More formal ways to integrate statistical tests across the constituent studies of a theoretically structured meta-study, including how to weigh different evidence
How state organisation and capacity connect to electoral accountability beyond Brazilian municipalities
C00443.data_asset: a new validated measure of bureaucratic quality across Brazilian municipalities combined with replication data from studies of audits, voter updating and incumbency disadvantage
C00443.scope: Illustrated for Brazilian mayors only, on qualitative congruence across four studies; the incumbency-disadvantage test is only marginally significant and larger at low and high bureaucratic quality.

C01241.claim: Longer NREGS exposure before the 2009 election cut the probability that the UPA government won a polling station by 19pp (RD); the drop comes from poorly implemented areas, with gains in well-implemented ones.
C01241.treatment_desc: longer exposure to India's NREGS workfare programme: phase 1 districts (two full agricultural off-seasons before the 2009 election) versus phase 2 districts (one), assigned by a state-quota poverty-ranking algorithm
C01241.outcome_desc: probability that the UPA government coalition receives the most votes at a polling station in the 2009 Indian general election (also at parliamentary constituency level)

magnitudes.outcome: probability UPA wins the most votes at a polling station, phase 1 vs phase 2 at
probability UPA wins the parliamentary constituency (collapsed data)
probability UPA wins the most votes, nonstar (low implementation quality) states
probability UPA wins the most votes, star (high implementation quality) states

setting.unit_desc: polling stations (close to 600,000 digitised for the 2009 general election, estimation uses a window around the cutoff) in districts assigned to NREGS phases 1 and 2

identification.variation: state-specific discontinuities in NREGS phase assignment, since each state's district quota was filled by a poverty ranking (fuzzy RD, local randomisation and parametric estimators)
identification.threat: comparability of phase 1 and 2 districts at the cutoff (baseline economic and political balance tests); not all alternative explanations of the mechanism can be ruled out

mechanisms.note: most plausible channel: voters hold the government accountable for implementation quality, as the decline is concentrated in low-quality areas; reciprocity and rising awareness are not supported

settled: Governments often use short-run pre-election strategies, frequently with success (Akhmedov and Zhuravskaya 2004; Brender and Drazen 2005; Healy and Lenz 2014; Shi and Svensson 2006)
In developing countries programmes often suffer low awareness and poor implementation, and short-run reelection strategies work especially well (Finan and Schechter 2012; Brender and Drazen 2008)
contested: Whether longer programme exposure raises or lowers incumbent support: reciprocity and awareness predict gains; loss of salience, disappointment or identity voting predict declines or nothing
Whether longer exposure helps incumbents, as De la O (2013) finds for Progresa in Mexico, or hurts them, as found here for NREGS
gaps: Medium-run electoral effects of longer programme exposure, which the paper calls understudied
Whether the implementation-quality accountability channel can be separated from loss of salience and other explanations that cannot be fully ruled out
C01241.data_asset: newly digitised polling-station results for the 2009 Indian general election merged with 2003 Planning Commission poverty ranks, 2001 Census population and NREGS phase
C01241.scope: Identified at the phase 1 versus phase 2 cutoff; the decline is driven by nonstar (poorly implemented) states while star states see gains; migration rises in phase 1 districts.

C01119.claim: Expressway expansion raised the ruling AKP's vote share in Turkish provinces (4.8pp for the average province, a third of its 2002-2011 gain), mainly at the CHP's expense, via visibility and signalled competence, not local growth.
C01119.treatment_desc: length of the expressway network built in a province by the AKP government's national programme (province-by-year variation, 2000-2018)
C01119.outcome_desc: AKP vote share in the province in seven elections between 2002 and 2015

magnitudes.outcome: AKP vote share, average province (expressway network from 51 to 193 km)
AKP vote share per 10% increase in expressway length

setting.unit_desc: 81 Turkish provinces; novel expressway length data 2000-2018 from the General Directorate of Highways; vote results for seven elections 2002-2015

identification.variation: province-by-year variation in expressway length with province and year fixed effects; parallel-trends assumption conditional on region-specific quadratic trends and time-varying controls
identification.threat: expressways could be targeted to provinces on different AKP vote trends or be spatially clustered; checked with leads, region and province trends, controls for other AKP investments, heterogeneous-effects estimators, spatial SEs and a dynamic instrument

mechanisms.note: visibility of the project drove votes: larger effects in discontented, poorer and less educated provinces, while less visible but economically successful investments (natural gas) had no effect
expressways signalled competence, persuading voters to switch allegiance without measurable local economic gains

settled: Democratisation promotes growth, with elections working through voters holding politicians accountable for public goods (Besley 2006; Acemoglu et al. 2019)
Persuading voters at scale is difficult (Kalla and Broockman 2018; DellaVigna and Gentzkow 2010)
contested: Whether infrastructure wins votes through local economic gains or through the visibility and competence it signals (Meyersson 2017 finds the AKP's rise was not primarily driven by growth)
Whether large visible projects only consolidate power in autocracies or can also persuade new voters in electoral democracies
gaps: Whether the economic effects of expressways arrive with a lag and later explain vote gains, which the contemporaneous economic-channel tests could miss
C01119.data_asset: novel administrative data on expressway length by province, 2000-2018, matched to province-level results of seven elections 2002-2015
C01119.scope: Competitive elections in Turkey 2002-2015; effects larger in provinces with more political and economic discontent in the 1990s-2001 and in less educated, poorer provinces; no significant turnout change.

C01120.claim: Brazil's Luz para Todos rural electrification had no effect on the PT's 2006 vote but raised its presidential vote share from 2010 (+3.8pp) through 2022, with education spillovers as the lagged channel.
C01120.treatment_desc: Luz para Todos rural electrification (from 2004), allocated to municipalities with under 85% of households connected in the 2000 census (ITT and fuzzy RD)
C01120.outcome_desc: PT candidates' vote share in presidential elections at municipality level, 2002-2022; individual-level propensity to vote for the PT in 2006 and 2010

magnitudes.outcome: PT vote share in the 2010 presidential election, municipalities eligible for LPT

setting.unit_desc: Brazilian municipalities around the 85% household-electrification eligibility threshold; individual-level survey of 2010 respondents; sample sizes not in the slices

identification.variation: eligibility rule: municipalities with fewer than 85% of households with electricity in the 2000 census qualified for the programme, used as ITT and as an instrument in a fuzzy RD
identification.threat: the assumption that the programme was implemented under quasi-experimental rules, with no manipulation of the threshold (tested, no self-selection); bandwidth sensitivity checked

mechanisms.note: returns arrive only after policy spillovers on education (school attendance, evening classes) widen the pool of beneficiaries and let the incumbent claim credit, so the effect lags several years

settled: Democracy and enfranchisement are associated with higher electrification supply in Sub-Saharan Africa (Trotter 2016; Kroth et al. 2016)
Electricity coverage expansions follow election cycles in India (Min 2015; Baskaran et al. 2015)
contested: Whether and when large infrastructure investments pay electoral returns, given short-term costs, uncertain political returns and myopic voters
Which conditions matter for returns: concentration of costs and benefits, effective implementation, or policy spillovers through other policies
gaps: Marginal electoral returns of programmatic infrastructure relative to more targeted mobilisation strategies in developing countries, and how the two interact
Whether the finding that infrastructure and clientelism act as substitutes generalises beyond Brazil's PT, which lacked rural broker networks
How highly competitive environments handle the short-term transition costs of moving from clientelism to programmatic strategies

C00886.claim: Primaries are most valuable in one-party-dominant districts: more competitive there, they select high-quality candidates in open seats and punish scandal-hit incumbents (nearly 20% chance of losing in safe districts).
C00886.treatment_desc: partisan safety of the constituency: one party's clear advantage in voter loyalties, versus competitive two-party districts
C00886.outcome_desc: quality of primary winners and probability that low-quality or scandal-hit incumbents lose the primary, in safe vs competitive districts

magnitudes.outcome: probability (%) a scandal-hit incumbent in a safe district loses the primary, 'n

setting.unit_desc: US House and Senate races and the North Carolina state legislature; about 60% of congressional districts are dominated by one party

identification.variation: cross-district variation in the partisan advantage of the constituency, comparing primary competitiveness and the fate of low-quality or scandal-hit incumbents in safe vs competitive districts
identification.threat: primary vote-share losses may matter little since incumbents win primaries by larger margins than general elections; unclear what information voters have about outcomes

mechanisms.note: primaries in safe, open-seat constituencies select high-quality candidates
primaries punish poor performance, such as scandals, by incumbents of the dominant party

settled: Almost all candidates for major US elected offices are nominated in direct primary elections
Scandals typically hurt incumbents' vote shares (studies of scandals and primary outcomes)
contested: Whether primaries raise politician quality at all: textbooks echo Turner's (1953) verdict that they are not a successful alternative to two-party competition
Whether quality gains from primaries are offset by pulling politicians away from the median voter, as a large literature may suggest
gaps: The full costs and benefits of primaries as an additional hurdle in the electoral process
What information voters actually have about politicians' outcomes and quality when they vote in primaries
C00886.data_asset: primary election results and candidate quality indicators (office experience, endorsements, scandals, spending) for US House, Senate and state legislative races
C00886.scope: strongest in constituencies dominated by one party and in open-seat races; primaries may also matter in competitive districts when polarization is high

C01551.claim: Women from historically more pastoral societies are more likely to have been infibulated, hold stricter norms on promiscuity and have less freedom of mobility; IV supports causality, with male absence as the channel.
C01551.treatment_desc: historical dependence on pastoralism of the woman's ancestral ethnic group (Ethnographic Atlas), instrumented by ecological suitability for pastoralism
C01551.outcome_desc: infibulation (the most invasive female genital cutting), norms about women's promiscuity, and restrictions on women's freedom of mobility

setting.unit_desc: about 500,000 women from 275 ethnic groups in 34 or 35 countries across Africa, Asia, Europe and South America (abstract and text differ on the count)

identification.variation: within-country variation across women by their ethnic group's historical pastoralism, instrumented by land suitability for pastoralism relative to agriculture
identification.threat: pastoralism may proxy for male dominance, plough use or historical development; tested with plough, non-herding animal husbandry, polygyny and kinship-tightness controls

mechanisms.note: a historical subsistence mode shaped norms that restrict women's sexuality and persist today, through male absence and paternity uncertainty

settled: Anthropologists have long argued that modes of economic production shape societal phenomena such as female status (Boserup 1970; Sanday 1973, 1981; Aberle 1973)
Historical experiences shape present variation in norms and trust (Heldring 2018; Nunn and Wantchekon 2011; Lowes and Montero 2018)
contested: Whether restrictions on women's sexuality stem from male absence under pastoralism, male dominance per se, or historical development; the paper finds male absence
gaps: Why persistence of restrictive norms weakens over time and whether it depends on the persistence of pastoralism itself
C01551.data_asset: individual survey data on about 500,000 women linked to ancestral pastoralism (Ethnographic Atlas, 1,202 societies) and land suitability for pastoralism
C01551.scope: within-country differences across women of different ethnic ancestry; male absence rather than male dominance or development is the channel; persistence weakens over time (initial evidence)
