C01623.claim: Chinese civilization formed through cultural hegemony: an elite bronze-ritual culture centred on ancestral offerings crystallised at Erlitou in the early second millennium BCE and spread by the early Shang.
C01623.treatment_desc: an elite ritual culture centred on bronze vessels and ancestral offerings (cultural hegemony) as opposed to dynastic state formation
C01623.outcome_desc: formation of Chinese civilization, marked by the spread of bronze vessels with common motifs and ritual forms across the Chinese continental region

setting.unit_desc: archaeological bronze assemblages from Erlitou (Yanshi, Henan) and the Central Plains, early second millennium BCE through the Western Zhou

identification.variation: archaeological and textual analysis of Erlitou bronzes, ritual forms and their spread; no estimated effect
identification.threat: traditional historical texts are largely mythical and there is no contemporaneous written evidence tying Erlitou to the Xia

mechanisms.note: elites of other cultures emulated the offering rites first associated with the Central Plains, anticipating the later common elite culture defined by shared rites

settled: The historicity of the Shang dynasty, or at least its last capital, was confirmed by the 1920s discovery of the Remains of Yin near Anyang
Much of the traditional historical record is mythical in character and unreliable as a basis for historical reconstruction (the author's earlier work)
contested: Whether Erlitou culture represents the Xia dynasty, as many archaeologists take it, given no contemporaneous written evidence
Whether Erlitou was a 'state' (Liu Li and Chen Xingcan 2003) or the origin of a cultural hegemony, as the paper argues
gaps: Whether the Xia, the earliest hereditary dynasty in the records, was historical, an open question since the Shang's historicity was validated
How to match the Xia of the historical records to the archaeological evidence absent contemporaneous written evidence
C01623.data_asset: archaeological evidence from Erlitou bronzes with common motifs and ritual forms, later Shang and Zhou bronze assemblages, and traditional historical texts
C01623.scope: bronze ritual forms mark an elite culture with continuity from Erlitou to Erligang and from late Shang to Zhou; cultural diversity and local political authority remained

C02506.claim: Darwin's reading shifted from early exploitation to later exploration, seeking unusually high cognitive surprise, along a path far more exploratory than the culture's production of books; shifts match epochs of his career.
C02506.treatment_desc: stage of Darwin's career: early vs later reading, with shift points detected by an unsupervised Bayesian model
C02506.outcome_desc: information-theoretic surprise (KL divergence) of each book relative to the previous book (text-to-text) and to all past reading (text-to-past)

setting.unit_desc: one scholar, Charles Darwin; full text of the books listed in his chronologically organised reading notebooks

identification.variation: topic models (k = 80) of book texts; KL-divergence surprise of each book vs the previous book and vs past reading; compared with a null model and a greedy shortest path
identification.threat: Darwin's early exploitation may have followed an earlier exploration phase before 1837 that the notebooks do not record

settled: Search under uncertainty involves a trade-off between exploiting past discoveries and exploring new domains (March 1991; Pirolli and Card 1999)
Scholars can be viewed as conducting cognitive search, balancing novel ideas against domains they already know (Todd et al. 2012; Berger-Tal et al. 2014)
contested: Whether exploitation then exploration fits optimal-agent models (Gittins 1979), which predict the reverse order, unless Darwin explored before 1837
gaps: Whether the exploitation-then-exploration pattern holds for other scientists in other eras, and how they relate to culture as a whole
What Darwin's research plans were in the period of relative uncertainty around 1846, between the detected boundary and his recorded start date
C02506.data_asset: full text of books listed in Darwin's chronologically organised reading notebooks, topic-modelled with 80 topics
C02506.scope: a single scholar; shifts coincide with biographically significant epochs; text-to-text boundary at 16 September 1854, text-to-past boundary at 27 May 1846; robust to 20, 40 and 60 topics

C00990.claim: A narrow left-wing mayoral victory in Colombia raises right-wing paramilitary violence in the next term by up to 7.3 events per 100,000 inhabitants a year, almost one standard deviation: elites offset outsiders' access.
C00990.treatment_desc: narrow election of a left-wing (outsider) mayor vs a narrow loss, in Colombian municipal elections
C00990.outcome_desc: yearly violent events by right-wing paramilitary groups per 100,000 inhabitants in the municipality during the subsequent government term

magnitudes.outcome: yearly paramilitary violent events per 100,000 inhabitants, up to
casualties per 100,000 from paramilitary violent events, lower estimate
casualties per 100,000 from paramilitary violent events, upper estimate

setting.unit_desc: Colombian municipalities with close elections between left-wing and other mayoral candidates

identification.variation: close mayoral elections in which a left-wing candidate narrowly wins or loses, using the vote margin at zero with an optimal bandwidth
identification.threat: manipulation of the running variable, checked with a density test showing no jump at the threshold, and sensitivity to bandwidths from 0.05 to 0.15

mechanisms.note: when outsiders win formal power, elites with de facto power (paramilitaries) use violence to offset their access

settled: Despite nominally democratic institutions, some groups stay excluded from power through clientelism, unequal resources, violence and participation barriers (Baland and Robinson 2008; Naidu 2012)
Excluded groups often resort to violence to express their views and influence policy
contested: Whether giving excluded groups formal power cuts violence, as Przeworski (1991) and Regan and Henderson (2002) argue, or raises it; findings on elections and conflict are mixed
gaps: Under what conditions the election of previously excluded outsiders triggers more or less violence, which mixed findings leave unresolved
C00990.data_asset: municipal election results (compiled by Pachon and Sanchez) matched with municipal violent events by paramilitary, guerrilla and government actors per 100,000 inhabitants
C00990.scope: narrow left-wing victories at the RD threshold, over the subsequent government term; robust to alternative violence measures; positive for bandwidths 0.05 to 0.15

C01372.claim: Wage under-reporting by formal Mexican firms is extensive; a 1997 pension reform tying benefits to reported wages for younger workers led to a relative decline in under-reporting for younger age groups.
C01372.treatment_desc: 1997 Mexican pension reform tying pension benefits more closely to reported wages for younger workers than for older workers
C01372.outcome_desc: wage under-reporting by formal firms: gap between wages firms report to the social security agency (IMSS) and wages workers report in a household labor-force survey

setting.unit_desc: formal firms' wage reports to IMSS compared with household labor-force survey responses, by worker age group, firm size and sector

identification.variation: the 1997 pension reform tied benefits to reported wages more for younger than for older workers; under-reporting compared across age groups before and after
identification.threat: IMSS-survey wage discrepancies might not reflect evasion; the reform's effect supports reading them as evasion; workers' awareness of under-reporting is unknown

mechanisms.note: enlisting workers through benefit-wage links raises compliance and fiscal capacity where third-party employer reporting is unreliable

settled: Weak fiscal capacity, especially difficulty raising taxes, constrains economic performance in developing countries (Burgess and Stern 1993; Besley and Persson 2013)
Third-party employer reporting of wages works well in rich countries: about 1% of US wages and salaries went unreported vs 57% of non-farm proprietor income (IRS 2006; Slemrod 2007)
contested: Whether third-party employer wage reports stay accurate in developing countries with weak enforcement: the paper finds substantial under-reporting in Mexico
gaps: Whether more pressure on firms to report accurately pushes more firms to stay informal, cutting compliance on the extensive margin
Effects of the pension reform on the informal/formal employment margin, left for future work
How far workers know of employers' under-reporting, and whether the reform works through incentives or information
C01372.data_asset: matched firm wage reports to the social security agency (IMSS) and household labor-force survey (ENEU) responses, with links to a Mexican establishment survey
C01372.scope: under-reporting is extensive and compliance is better in larger firms; the effect is a relative decline for younger vs older workers, on the intensive margin among registered firms

C00746.claim: Cooperatives created by El Salvador's 1980 land reform specialise in staples rather than cash crops, are less productive in cash crops but more in staples, and pay members more equally than outside-owned haciendas.
C00746.treatment_desc: 1980 land reform converting properties of owners above a 500 ha cumulative landholding threshold into cooperatives, vs outside-owned haciendas below it
C00746.outcome_desc: staple-crop specialization: likelihood of producing staples and land share in staples rather than cash crops (2007 agricultural census); also productivity and worker earnings

setting.unit_desc: agricultural properties (cooperatives and haciendas) near the 500 ha cumulative landholding threshold

identification.variation: discontinuous probability of cooperative formation at the 500 ha cumulative landholding threshold of the 1980 land reform, with MSE-optimal bandwidths
identification.threat: landholders might sort around the threshold to avoid expropriation (no evidence found); selection bias in yields addressed with a Heckman correction

mechanisms.note: members jointly decide one member, one vote; staple specialization and equal pay are consistent with the model but not a definitive test

settled: Property rights institutions are central to economic development, and ownership structures vary widely across the world (Alchian and Demsetz 1972; Hansmann 1996)
A rich theoretical literature links ownership structure to specialization, efficiency and equity
contested: Whether the allocation of property rights matters for specialization, efficiency and equity: theory is rich but causal evidence is limited because property rights are endogenous
gaps: Impacts of cooperative ownership on individuals, using linked administrative data
Political consequences of cooperative formation, using political data
How social norms shape the success of cooperatives
C00746.data_asset: 2007 agricultural census and household earnings data linked to cooperative status from the 1980 land reform by cumulative landholding
C00746.scope: local to properties near the 500 ha threshold; cooperatives are less productive in cash crops, more in staples, with higher incomes and more equal wages for members

C01377.claim: In Mexico City higher property tax rates and enforcement letters both raise revenue; rate hikes raise welfare, while enforcement lowers it as threat costs exceed revenue gains.
C01377.treatment_desc: sharp property tax rate increases across cadastral value bands, and a field experiment sending enforcement letters to delinquent taxpayers
C01377.outcome_desc: property tax revenue and compliance (payment) of residential properties in Mexico City

magnitudes.outcome: total property tax revenue, collective variation studied
elasticity of tax revenue to the tax rate, 9.1 basis point change
elasticity of tax revenue to the tax rate, 18.0 basis point change

setting.unit_desc: universe of residential properties in Mexico City, from administrative property tax records

identification.variation: sharp changes in property tax rates across cadastral value bands compared before and after, plus a randomised enforcement-letter experiment; elasticities feed an optimal tax model
identification.threat: exemptions for about 7 percent of properties and a change in band thresholds in 2008-09; results are robust to dropping exempt properties

settled: The property tax is the most under-utilised tax in developing countries
contested: Whether higher tax rates or more enforcement is the better way to raise property tax revenue: here rate hikes raise welfare while enforcement lowers it
gaps: Optimal design of loans for liquidity-constrained taxpayers: eligibility, interest rates and payment schedules
Applying the tax-systems approach to other settings and studying the roles of tax fairness and equity
C01377.data_asset: administrative tax records for the universe of residential properties in Mexico City, with tax rate changes and an enforcement-letter field experiment
C01377.scope: Mexico City, similar to other developing countries in liquidity constraints and administrative capacity; larger rate changes may trigger more-than-proportional compliance drops

C02199.claim: Attitudes toward eliminating big income inequalities in 25 EU states reflect political and social attitudes, notably the importance of merit, as well as economic factors such as education; merit matters in 20 of 25 countries.
C02199.treatment_desc: individual political attitudes (old Left vs old Right), economic self-interest (e.g. education) and general social attitudes such as the importance of recognising merit
C02199.outcome_desc: stated importance of eliminating big income inequalities between citizens (ordered response), World Values and European Values Surveys 2000-1

mechanisms.note: economic utilitarian factors such as education matter, but political and social attitudes, especially merit, matter too, so ideas shape redistribution attitudes beyond self-interest

settled: National economic and social context, such as the level of inequality and the type of welfare state, is the usual explanation for variation in attitudes toward inequality

Whether attitudes toward inequality come from economic self-interest or from ideas: political and social attitudes, especially merit, matter alongside education
C02199.data_asset: 2000-1 wave of the World Values and European Values Surveys, respondents in 25 EU member states
C02199.scope: effects vary across countries: merit is positive and significant in 20 of 25, old Left vs Right in 12 of 25 and gender in 9 of 25

C01895.claim: In a 1911 cross-section of 1,274 gas companies, municipal ownership was likelier in small towns and under city-council regulation and less likely under state commissions, supporting small-market and commitment explanations.
C01895.treatment_desc: regulatory regime of the gas company: regulation by city councils vs by state commissions vs unregulated, plus town size
C01895.outcome_desc: whether a gas company was municipally (publicly) owned rather than privately owned in 1911

setting.unit_desc: 1,274 public and private gas companies operating in 1911, with state laws on municipal ownership, rate regulation and commissions

identification.variation: cross-section of gas companies comparing ownership by town size and by regulatory regime, using state laws authorizing municipal regulation or creating state commissions

mechanisms.note: municipal regulation raised the risk to private capital so towns took over; state regulation was less burdensome and reduced municipal ownership

settled: Public ownership is a common organisational form, especially for utilities such as water and sewer, and arises where non-redeployable capital is important
Secure property rights are widely believed necessary for private capital formation, though this was largely untested
contested: Whether state regulation substantially affected utility rates: early studies found little effect, but Meyer and Leland (1980) find sometimes substantial effects
Whether public ownership reflects small markets, commitment problems or patronage: the tests favour small markets and commitment

C01895.data_asset: cross-section of 1,274 public and private gas companies in 1911, with state laws on municipal ownership, rate regulation and utility commissions

C02014.claim: Review: research explains how regional and international currency regimes emerge and evolve, and, domestically, how economic interests and political institutions shape governments' exchange rate policy choices.
C02014.treatment_desc: economic interests and political institutions as determinants of exchange rate policy, alongside the international monetary system
C02014.outcome_desc: exchange rate policy: the international and regional currency regime and the national regime and level chosen by governments

setting.unit_desc: handbook chapter surveying the international monetary system over the past two centuries and national exchange rate policies

identification.variation: literature review of the political economy of exchange rates, at the global and national levels

At the domestic level there are reasonably well-developed arguments about the economic interests at stake and how political institutions affect currency policy choices

How international regime conditions affect domestic lobbying over exchange rates

C02042.claim: Trade openness and firm mobility pushed US senators toward restricting low-skill immigration after 1950, as immigrant-using firms closed or moved abroad and stopped lobbying for open immigration.
C02042.treatment_desc: US trade openness and other states' openness to foreign direct investment (firm mobility), after 1950
C02042.outcome_desc: US senators' roll-call votes on low-skill immigration policy (voting for more open immigration)

identification.variation: over-time changes in trade openness and world capital openness related to senators' votes on immigration, with controls for party, nativism, unions and welfare spending
identification.threat: endogeneity of immigration policy to trade and the strategic roll-call vote-generating process; mitigated by using Congress's immigration votes after 1950 and all Senate votes

Trade effects on firms are modelled through factor intensity (Ricardo-Viner) and productivity differences (Melitz) as separate channels

Whether trade exposure and production location also shape firms' preferences over other foreign economic policies and domestic labor, welfare and environmental policies
C02042.data_asset: roll-call votes on immigration in the US Senate after 1950, matched to trade openness, world capital openness and industry lobbying on low-skill immigration
C02042.scope: US Senate after 1950; trade openness has a negative, significant effect in all models; Republicans show a slightly positive firm-mobility effect via subsidies to agricultural firms

C02734.claim: Employer political requests raised US workers' self-reported participation around the 2014 election (0.77 more civic acts) and were roughly as effective as union or party contact, especially with job-loss warnings and monitoring.
C02734.treatment_desc: employer political requests: contact from employers asking employees to act politically, compared with union and party contact; job-loss warnings and monitoring as moderators

Whether worker fears of economic insecurity, including threats of sanctions, lower the costs of employer recruitment, especially partisan recruitment

C02734.scope: stronger when employers warn of job loss, moderated by county unemployment, and can monitor employees; roughly as effective as union and party contact

C01013.claim: FM radio defection messages aimed at the LRA raised defections and cut fatalities (-2.7% per 1-sd rise in messaging intensity), violence against civilians and clashes with security forces.

returnees, per 1-sd rise in defection messaging intensity
fatalities, 60+ minutes of messaging at full cell coverage

After ineffective macro-level peace agreements in the early 1990s, policy turned to individual incentives to participate in violence

far-right vote share, Vienna wards with majority in public housing
change in far-right support, high public housing vs lower diversity, 2002-6
